Athens at least is a near neighbor, and still you utterly ignore her. Against Athens you choose defense over attack, and you leave the outcome to chance by postponing the struggle until she is far stronger than she was. And you know that, on the whole, the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself, and that if Athens, our present enemy, has not many times destroyed us, we owe that more to her blunders than to your protection. Indeed, hopes placed in you have before now ruined some, whose faith made them neglect to prepare.

“We hope none of you will take this remonstrance as hostility. Men remonstrate with friends who are mistaken; accusations they keep for enemies who have wronged them. Besides, we think we have as good a right as anyone to point out a neighbor’s faults, particularly in view of the great contrast between the two national characters. As far as we can tell, you hardly perceive this contrast. You have never yet considered what kind of opponents the Athenians will be, or how widely and completely they differ from you. The Athenians are addicted to innovation, and quick both in forming a design and in carrying it out. You have a genius for keeping what you have, and you have no inventiveness whatever; when forced to act, you never go far enough. They are adventurous beyond their power and daring beyond their judgment, and they stay hopeful in danger. You attempt less than your power allows, distrust even what your judgment approves, and think there is no escape from danger. They act promptly where you put things off. They are always abroad, and you never leave home. They hope that being away will add to their gains; you fear that advancing will put at risk what you left behind. They press a success quickly, and they are slow to fall back from a reverse. They spend their bodies freely for their country; their intellect they keep jealously for her service. A plan left unexecuted is to them a real loss, and a successful enterprise something of a failure. If an undertaking fails, fresh hopes soon make up the lack. They alone can call a thing hoped for a thing gained, because they act on their resolutions so fast. So they labor on through trouble and danger all their lives, with little chance to enjoy anything, always occupied in getting. Their idea of a holiday is to do what the moment requires, and hard work seems to them less of a misfortune than the peace of a quiet life. In a word, one might truly say that they were born to take no rest themselves and to allow none to others.

“That is Athens, your antagonist. And still, Lacedaemonians, you delay. You do not see that peace lasts longest for those who take as much care to show they will not submit to injustice as to use their power justly. Your notion of fair dealing is quite different. You hold that by doing no harm to others you avoid having to risk your own fortunes to stop others from harming you. You could hardly have succeeded with such a policy even beside a neighbor like yourselves. As we have just shown, against Athens your ways are out of date. In politics, as in the arts, new methods always win out. Fixed customs serve best for communities left in peace, but those under constant necessity of action need constantly improved methods. That is why Athens, with her vast experience, has gone further than you along the road of innovation.

“Let your delay end here, at least. Help your allies now, and Potidæa above all, as you promised, by invading Attica quickly. Do not hand friends and kindred over to their bitterest enemies, and so drive the rest of us in despair to another alliance. Neither the Gods who received our oaths nor the men who witnessed them would condemn that step. When desertion forces a people to seek new ties, the broken treaty is not their fault but the fault of the power that fails to help its confederate. If you will only act, we will stand by you. It would be unnatural for us to change, and we should never find so congenial an ally. For these reasons, choose the right course, and take care that Peloponnese under your supremacy does not fall short of the prestige it held under your ancestors.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. Athenian envoys happened to be at Lacedaemon on other business. When they heard the speeches, they felt they ought to appear before the Lacedaemonians. They did not mean to defend themselves against the charges the cities were bringing. They meant to show, taking the whole situation into view, that the matter should not be decided in haste but needed more consideration. They also wished to point out the great power of Athens, to remind the old of what they knew and inform the young of what they did not, thinking their words might lead the Lacedaemonians to prefer tranquility to war. So they approached the Lacedaemonians and said that, if there was no objection, they too wished to address the assembly. The Lacedaemonians told them to come forward. The Athenians stepped up and spoke as follows:

“We did not come here to argue with your allies. We came on the business our state sent us to attend to. But the vehemence of the outcry against us has persuaded us to speak. We will not answer the accusations of the cities (you are not, in any case, the judges before whom we or they can plead). We want to keep you from taking the wrong course on weighty matters by giving in too readily to your allies’ persuasion. We also want to show, by going over the whole indictment, that we hold our possessions by a fair title and that our country deserves consideration. We need not go back to remote antiquity, where we could cite tradition but not what our hearers have seen. But we must refer to the Median War and to recent history, though we are rather tired of raising the subject again and again. In that war we took great risks to gain certain advantages. You shared in the solid results, so do not try to deny us every share in whatever good the glory may do us. Still, we tell the story not so much to deprecate hostility as to bear witness against it, and to show what sort of antagonist Athens is likely to prove, if you are so ill advised as to go to war with her. We say that at Marathon we stood in the front line and faced the barbarian alone. When he came a second time and we could not match him on land, we embarked on our ships with our whole people and fought at Salamis. That kept him from taking the Peloponnesian states one at a time and ravaging them with his fleet, since the number of his vessels would have made any joint defense impossible. The invader himself gave the best proof of this. Beaten at sea, he judged his power no longer what it had been, and withdrew as fast as he could with most of his army.

“That, then, was the outcome, and it was clearly shown that the cause of Hellas rested on her fleet. We supplied three very valuable things toward that outcome: the most ships, the ablest commander, and the most unhesitating patriotism. Our ships numbered little less than two-thirds of the four hundred in all. Our commander was Themistocles, who above all brought about the battle in the straits, universally acknowledged to have saved our cause. This is in fact why you honored him as you never honored any foreign visitor. In daring patriotism we had no rivals. No reinforcements came from behind us, and everything ahead of us was already conquered. Even so, we had the spirit to leave our city and give up our property (rather than desert the rest of the league or scatter and deprive them of our help), and to throw ourselves into our ships and face the danger, without a thought of resenting your failure to help us. We maintain, therefore, that we gave you as much as we received. You had something to fight for: the cities you had left were still full of your homes, and you could hope to enjoy them again. Your coming was prompted as much by fear for yourselves as for us. At any rate, you never appeared until we had nothing left to lose. We left behind a city that was no longer a city, and risked our lives for a city that existed only in desperate hope. So we took our full share in your deliverance and our own. If we had followed others, and let fear for our land make us side with the Mede before you came, or if our ruin had broken our spirit and kept us from boarding our ships, you would have been too weak at sea to fight, and he would have gained his ends without a struggle.

“Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither the patriotism we showed in that crisis nor the wisdom of our counsels earns us our extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes, at least not for our empire. We did not win that empire by violence. You were unwilling to see the war against the barbarian through to the end, and the allies came over to us and asked us themselves to take the command. Then the nature of the case forced us to build our empire up to its present height, fear being our chief motive, with honor and interest following. And in the end, when nearly everyone hated us, when some had already revolted and been put down, and when you were no longer the friends you had been but objects of suspicion and dislike, it no longer seemed safe to give up our empire, especially since all who left us would go over to you. And no one can blame a people for making the best provision it can for its interest when the risks are tremendous.

“You, Lacedaemonians, at any rate, have used your supremacy to settle the states of Peloponnese in the way that suits you. If at the time we speak of you had stayed with the matter to the end, and had become hated in command, we are sure you would have been just as galling to the allies, and would have had to choose between firm government and danger to yourselves. It follows that we did nothing very remarkable, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, when we accepted an empire that was offered to us and then refused to give it up. Three of the strongest motives, fear, honor and interest, forced us. Nor were we the first to set this example, for it has always been the rule that the weaker is subject to the stronger. Besides, we thought ourselves worthy of our position, and so did you until now, when calculations of interest have made you raise the cry of justice. No one has ever yet put justice forward to stop his own ambition when he had a chance to gain something by force. All praise is due to those who, though not so far above human nature as to refuse dominion, still respect justice more than their position requires.

“We think our moderation would be best shown if others stood in our place. Yet even our fairness has brought us, most unreasonably, condemnation instead of approval. We have waived some of our rights in contract suits with our allies and let impartial laws at Athens decide them, and for this we have the name of being litigious. No one asks why other imperial powers are not reproached in this way, though they treat their subjects less moderately than we do. The secret is that where force can be used, there is no need of law. But our subjects are so accustomed to dealing with us as equals that they resent every defeat that goes against their notions of justice, whether it comes from a legal judgment or from the power our empire gives us. They forget to be grateful that they keep most of their possessions, and they are angrier at the loss of a part than if we had set law aside from the start and openly indulged our covetousness. Had we done that, not even they would have denied that the weaker must yield to the stronger. Men, it seems, are angrier at legal wrong than at violent wrong. The first looks like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior. At any rate they endured much worse treatment from the Mede, yet they find our rule severe. That is to be expected, for the present always weighs heavily on the conquered. One thing at least is certain. If you overthrew us and took our place, you would soon lose the goodwill that fear of us has won you, if your policy today is anything like the sample you gave during your short command against the Mede. Your life at home is governed by rules and institutions that cannot agree with those of others, and abroad your citizens follow neither those rules nor the ones the rest of Hellas recognizes.

“Take time, then, to form your resolution, for the matter is a great one. Do not let the opinions and complaints of others persuade you to bring trouble on yourselves. Consider, before you are in it, how much accident counts in war. As a war goes on, it usually turns into a matter of chances, and neither of us is exempt from them; we must risk the outcome blindly. It is a common mistake in going to war to start at the wrong end, to act first and to discuss the matter only after disaster has come. But we are not yet so misguided, and, as far as we can see, neither are you. So while both of us can still choose rightly, we bid you not to dissolve the treaty or break your oaths, but to settle our differences by arbitration, as our agreement provides. If you refuse, we call to witness the gods who heard the oaths. If you begin hostilities, we will try, whatever course you take, not to be slow in repelling you.”

Such were the words of the Athenians. When the Lacedaemonians had heard the allies’ complaints against the Athenians and the Athenians’ remarks in reply, they had everyone leave and discussed the question among themselves. The majority all reached the same conclusion: the Athenians were plainly the aggressors, and war must be declared at once. But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, who had a reputation as a wise and moderate man, stepped forward and made this speech:

“Lacedaemonians, I have lived long enough to have seen many wars. I see men of my own age among you, who will not fall into the common misfortune of longing for war out of inexperience or out of a belief that it is advantageous and safe. If we look at it soberly, the war you are debating now would be one of the greatest magnitude. In a struggle with Peloponnesians and neighbors, our strength is of the same kind, and we can move swiftly to any point. But think of a struggle with a people who live far away, who are extraordinarily familiar with the sea, and who are in the highest state of preparation in every other respect. They have wealth, private and public, ships, horses, heavy infantry, and a population such as no other Hellenic place can match, and besides all this a number of tributary allies. What justifies us in rashly beginning such a struggle? What do we trust in, that we rush into it unprepared? Our ships? There we are inferior, and if we are to train and become their match, time must pass. Our money? There we are far worse off. We have none in our treasury, and we are not ready to contribute it from private funds. We might perhaps feel confident in our superiority in heavy infantry and numbers, which will allow us to invade and devastate their lands. But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can import what they need by sea. And if we try to stir up their allies to revolt, we shall have to support them with a fleet, since most of them are islanders. What, then, is our war to be? Unless we can beat them at sea, or cut them off from the revenues that feed their navy, we shall meet with little but disaster. Meanwhile our honor will be committed to going on, especially if people think we began the quarrel. Let us never be lifted up by the fatal hope that devastating their lands will end the war quickly. I fear rather that we may leave it as a legacy to our children, so unlikely is it that the Athenian spirit will be enslaved by its land, or Athenian experience cowed by war.

“I am not telling you to be so unfeeling as to let them injure your allies, or to refrain from exposing their intrigues. I am telling you not to take up arms at once. Send to them and remonstrate, in a tone neither too much like war nor too much like submission, and use the interval to complete our own preparations. We shall do this, first, by gaining allies, Hellenic or barbarian, it does not matter, provided they add to our strength in ships or in money — I say Hellenic or barbarian because the law of self-preservation removes any odium from such an addition, for all who, like us, are the targets of Athenian designs — and second, by developing our own resources. If they listen to our embassy, so much the better. If not, in two or three years our position will be considerably stronger, and we can attack them then, if we think fit. Perhaps by then the sight of our preparations, backed by language just as meaningful, will have inclined them to submit, while their land is still untouched and their counsels can still aim at keeping advantages not yet lost. You should regard their land only as a hostage in your hands, and the better it is cultivated, the more valuable a hostage. You ought to spare it as long as possible, and not make them desperate, which would make them harder to deal with. If, while we are unprepared, the complaints of our allies hurry us into laying it waste, beware that we do not bring deep disgrace and deep perplexity upon Peloponnese. Complaints, whether of communities or of individuals, can be settled. But a war undertaken by a coalition for the separate interests of its members, with a course no one can foresee, does not easily end in a creditable settlement.

“And no one need think it cowardice that a number of confederates hesitate before attacking a single city. The Athenians have allies as numerous as ours, and allies that pay tribute. War depends less on arms than on money, which makes arms useful, and this is truer than ever in a struggle between a land power and a sea power. So let us first provide money, and not be swept along by our allies’ talk before we have done so. We shall carry the largest share of responsibility for the consequences, good or bad, and therefore we also have the right to examine them calmly.

“As for the slowness and delay that they criticize most in us, you need not blush for them. If we go to war unprepared, we shall only delay its end by hurrying its beginning. Besides, ours has always been a free and famous city. What they condemn is really only a wise moderation. Because of it, we alone are not insolent in success, and we give way less than others in misfortune. We are not carried away by the pleasure of being cheered on to risks our judgment condemns, and when we are provoked, accusations meant to exasperate us do not persuade us any the more. We are both warlike and wise, and our sense of order makes us so. We are warlike because self-control has honor as a chief constituent, and honor has bravery. We are wise because we are brought up with too little learning to despise the laws and with too strict a self-control to disobey them. We are raised not to be too knowing in useless matters — such as the knowledge that can criticize an enemy’s plans plausibly in theory but cannot attack them with equal success in practice — and we are taught that our enemies’ schemes are much like our own, and that the freaks of chance cannot be settled by calculation. In practice we always prepare against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are good. Indeed, we should rest our hopes not on his blunders but on the soundness of our own provisions. And we should not suppose that one man differs much from another, but think that the advantage goes to the one reared in the strictest school. These practices, which our ancestors passed on to us and which have always profited us, must not be abandoned. We must not be hurried into deciding in one short day a question that concerns many lives, fortunes and cities, and in which honor is deeply involved. We must decide calmly, and our strength gives us a special ability to do so. As for the Athenians, send to them about Potidæa, send about the allies’ alleged wrongs, especially as they are ready to give legal satisfaction. Law forbids proceeding against one who offers arbitration as if he were a wrongdoer. Meanwhile do not neglect to prepare for war. This decision will be the best for yourselves and the most terrible for your opponents.”
That was the speech of Archidamus. Last to come forward was Sthenelaidas, one of the ephors for that year, who spoke to the Lacedaemonians as follows:

“I do not pretend to understand the long speech of the Athenians. They said a good deal in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are injuring our allies and Peloponnese. And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then, but ill toward us now, they deserve double punishment for having ceased to be good and for having become bad. We meanwhile are the same then and now. If we are wise, we shall not disregard the wrongs of our allies, or put off until tomorrow the duty of assisting those who must suffer today. Others have much money and ships and horses, but we have good allies, whom we must not give up to the Athenians. Nor must we decide the matter by lawsuits and words, since it is anything but in word that we are harmed; we must render instant and powerful help. And let us not be told that it is fitting for us to deliberate while under injustice. Long deliberation is rather fitting for those who have injustice in contemplation. Vote therefore, Lacedaemonians, for war, as the honor of Sparta demands. Neither allow the further aggrandizement of Athens, nor betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods let us advance against the aggressors.”

With these words he, as ephor, himself put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians. He said that he could not determine which was the loudest acclamation (their mode of decision is by acclamation, not by voting). In fact he wished to make them declare their opinion openly and so increase their ardor for war. Accordingly he said: “All Lacedaemonians who are of opinion that the treaty has been broken and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there,” pointing out a certain place; “all who are of the opposite opinion, there.” They stood up accordingly and divided, and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority. The Lacedaemonians then summoned the allies and told them that their opinion was that Athens had been guilty of injustice, but that they wished to convoke all the allies and put it to the vote, so that they might make war, if they decided to do so, on a common resolution. Having thus gained their point, the delegates returned home at once, and the Athenian envoys a little later, when they had dispatched the objects of their mission. This decision of the assembly, that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years’ truce, which was entered into after the affair of Euboea.

The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken and that the war must be declared. They did so not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies as because they feared the growth of the power of the Athenians, seeing most of Hellas already subject to them.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 4 — From the end of the Persian to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War—The Progress from Supremacy to Empire
paragraphs: This is how Athens came to be in the position from which her power grew. The Medes had returned from Europe, beaten by the Hellenes on sea and on land, and those who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been destroyed. Leotychides, king of the Lacedaemonians, who had commanded the Hellenes at Mycale, then went home with the allies from Peloponnese. The Athenians, however, and the allies from Ionia and Hellespont, who had by now revolted from the King, stayed behind and laid siege to Sestos, which the Medes still held. They wintered before it, and when the barbarians evacuated the place they took it. After this they sailed away from Hellespont, each to their own cities. Meanwhile the Athenian people, now that the barbarian had left their country, at once began to bring back their children and wives, and whatever property they had left, from the places where they had put it for safety, and prepared to rebuild their city and their walls. For only isolated stretches of the circuit had been left standing, and most of the houses were in ruins. A few remained, and these were the ones in which the Persian grandees had taken up their quarters.

The Lacedaemonians saw what the Athenians were about to do and sent an embassy to Athens. They would themselves have preferred that neither Athens nor any other city should have a wall, but in this they acted mainly at the urging of their allies, who were alarmed by the strength of her newly acquired navy and by the valor she had shown in the war with the Medes. They asked Athens not only to refrain from building walls for herself, but also to join them in pulling down the walls that were still standing in the cities outside Peloponnese. They did not declare the real meaning of their advice, which was suspicion of the Athenians. What they urged was that in the event of a third invasion the barbarian would then have no strong place to use as his base, as he now had in Thebes, and that Peloponnese would be enough for all as a base both for retreat and for attack. The Lacedaemonians spoke in this way, and on the advice of Themistocles the Athenians immediately sent them away with the answer that they would send ambassadors to Sparta to discuss the question. Themistocles told the Athenians to send him off to Lacedaemon with all speed, but not to dispatch his colleagues as soon as they had chosen them; they were to wait until they had raised the wall to the height from which defense was possible. In the meantime the whole population of the city was to work on the wall: the Athenians, their wives and their children, sparing no building, private or public, that could be of any use to the work, but tearing everything down. He gave these instructions and added that he would answer for everything else there, and then he left. When he arrived at Lacedaemon he did not seek an audience with the authorities, but tried to gain time and made excuses. Whenever anyone in the government asked him why he did not appear in the assembly, he said that he was waiting for his colleagues, who had been held up in Athens by some business; that he expected them to arrive soon, and wondered that they were not yet there. At first the Lacedaemonians believed Themistocles, because of their friendship for him. But when others arrived, all plainly declaring that the work was going on and was already rising to some height, they did not know how to disbelieve it. Aware of this, he told them that rumors are deceptive and should not be trusted; they should send some reputable men from Sparta to inspect the work and bring back a report that could be trusted. They dispatched them accordingly. Themistocles then sent secret word to the Athenians about these men, telling them to detain them as far as possible without putting them under open constraint, and not to let them go until he and his colleagues had returned. For his colleagues had now joined him, Abronichus, son of Lysicles, and Aristides, son of Lysimachus, with the news that the wall was high enough; and he feared that when the Lacedaemonians heard the facts, they might refuse to let him go. So the Athenians detained the envoys as his message had said, and Themistocles had his audience with the Lacedaemonians. At last he told them openly that Athens was now fortified well enough to protect its inhabitants. Any embassy that the Lacedaemonians or their allies might wish to send to Athens in future should proceed on the assumption that the people they were visiting could tell both its own interests and the general interests. When the Athenians had thought it right to abandon their city and embark in their ships, he said, they had taken that dangerous step without consulting the Lacedaemonians; and on the other hand, wherever they had deliberated together with the Lacedaemonians, they had proved themselves second to none in judgment. They now thought it right that their city should have a wall, and that this would be better for the citizens of Athens and for the Hellenic confederacy alike; for without equal military strength it was impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common interest. It followed, he observed, that either all the members of the confederacy should be without walls, or the present step should be accepted as right.

The Lacedaemonians showed no open anger against the Athenians at what they heard. Their embassy, it seems, had been meant not to obstruct, but to guide the counsels of the Athenian government. Besides, Spartan feeling toward Athens was at that time very friendly, because of the patriotism she had shown in the struggle with the Mede. Still, the defeat of their wishes could not fail to cause them secret annoyance. The envoys of each state went home without complaint.

So the Athenians walled their city in a short time, and the building still shows the haste with which it was done. The foundations consist of stones of every kind; in some places they are neither worked nor fitted, but set down just in the order in which the various workers brought them. Many columns from tombs and many sculptured stones were built in with the rest. The city’s bounds had been extended on every side, and so in their haste they seized on everything without exception. Themistocles also persuaded them to finish the walls of Piraeus, which had been begun earlier, in the year when he was archon. Two things influenced him: the excellence of a site with three natural harbors, and the great start the Athenians would gain in the acquisition of power by becoming a naval people. He was the first to venture to tell them to stick to the sea, and he began at once to lay the foundations of the empire. It was on his advice, too, that they built the walls as thick as they can still be seen around Piraeus; two wagons meeting each other brought up the stones. Inside the walls there was neither rubble nor mortar. They were built of great stones hewn square and fitted together, and clamped to each other on the outside with iron and lead. Only about half the height he intended was completed. He meant their size and thickness to keep off enemy attacks. A small garrison of invalids, he thought, would defend them adequately, and everyone else would be free for service in the fleet. For the fleet claimed most of his attention. He saw, as I think, that the king’s army would find the approach by sea easier than the approach by land, and he thought Piraeus more valuable than the upper city. Indeed, he was always advising the Athenians that if a day should come when land forces hard pressed them, they should go down into Piraeus and defy the world with their fleet. In this way the Athenians completed their wall, and they began their other buildings immediately after the retreat of the Mede.

Meanwhile Lacedaemon sent out Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, as commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, with twenty ships from Peloponnese. The Athenians sailed with him with thirty ships, and so did a number of the other allies. They made an expedition against Cyprus and subdued most of the island. Afterwards they attacked Byzantium, which the Medes held, and forced it to surrender. All this took place while the Spartans were still supreme. But the violence of Pausanias had already begun to be disagreeable to the Hellenes, above all to the Ionians and the newly liberated peoples. These went to the Athenians and asked them, as their kinsmen, to become their leaders and to check any attempt at violence by Pausanias. The Athenians accepted their proposals. They resolved to put down any attempt of the kind and to settle everything else as their interests might seem to require. In the meantime the Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias, to investigate the reports that had reached them. Hellenes arriving in Sparta had brought many grave accusations against him, and by all appearances he had acted more like a despot than like a general. His recall happened to come just when the hatred he had aroused had made the allies desert him and range themselves beside the Athenians; only the soldiers from Peloponnese stayed with him. On his arrival at Lacedaemon he was censured for his private acts of oppression, but he was acquitted on the heaviest counts and pronounced not guilty. It must be known that the charge of Medism was one of the principal articles against him, and by all appearances one of the best founded. Even so, the Lacedaemonians did not restore him to his command. They sent out Dorkis and certain others with a small force, but these found that the allies no longer wished to grant them the supremacy. They saw this and departed, and the Lacedaemonians sent no one out to succeed them. They feared that anyone who went out would deteriorate as Pausanias had. Besides, they wanted to be rid of the Median War, and they were satisfied that the Athenians were fit for the position and were at that time friendly to themselves.

Thus the Athenians had succeeded to the supremacy because the allies, hating Pausanias, gave it to them of their own will. They then fixed which cities should contribute money against the barbarian and which should contribute ships. The professed object was to retaliate for their sufferings by ravaging the King’s country. It was at this time that the Athenians first instituted the office of “Treasurers for Hellas.” These officers received the tribute, as the money contributed was called. The tribute was at first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents. The common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple. Their supremacy began with allies who were independent, and who acted on the resolutions of a common congress. Between the Median War and the present war, it was marked by the following undertakings in war and in administration: against the barbarian, against their own rebel allies, and against those Peloponnesian powers that came into contact with them on various occasions. I relate these events, and venture on this digression, for this reason: all my predecessors have left this part of history out, confining themselves either to Hellenic history before the Median War or to the Median War itself. Hellanicus, it is true, did touch on these events in his Athenian history, but he is rather brief and not accurate in his dates. Besides, the history of these events explains how the Athenian empire grew.

The Athenians, under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades, began by besieging and capturing Eion on the Strymon from the Medes, and they made slaves of its inhabitants. Next they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean with a Dolopian population, and colonized it themselves. A war against Carystus followed; the rest of Euboea stayed neutral, and the war ended with a surrender on conditions. After this Naxos left the confederacy. A war followed, and she was forced to return after a siege. This was the first case in which the terms of the alliance were broken by the subjugation of an allied city, and the others followed the precedent as circumstances dictated. Of all the causes of defection the chief was failure to pay tribute and supply ships, and failure to serve when called on. The Athenians were very severe and exacting, and they made themselves offensive by applying the screw of necessity to men who were not used to continuous labor, and in fact not disposed to it. In some other respects also the Athenians were no longer the popular rulers they had been at first. If they did more than their fair share of the service, it was correspondingly easy for them to reduce any who tried to leave the confederacy. The allies had themselves to blame for this. Most of them wished to get off service, and so arranged to pay their share of the expense in money in place of ships, in order to avoid leaving their homes. The result was that Athens increased her navy with the funds they contributed, while any revolt found them without resources or experience for war.

The next events were the actions by land and sea at the river Eurymedon, between the Athenians with their allies and the Medes. The Athenians won both battles on the same day under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades, and captured and destroyed the whole Phoenician fleet of two hundred vessels. Some time afterward the Thasians defected. The cause was disagreements about the markets on the opposite coast of Thrace and about the mine that they held. The Athenians sailed to Thasos with a fleet, defeated the Thasians at sea and landed on the island. About the same time they sent ten thousand settlers, drawn from their own citizens and the allies, to settle the place then called Ennea Hodoi or Nine Ways, and now Amphipolis. They won possession of Ennea Hodoi from the Edonians. But when they advanced into the interior of Thrace, the assembled Thracians cut them off at Drabescus, a town of the Edonians; the Thracians regarded the settlement of Ennea Hodoi as an act of hostility. Meanwhile the Thasians, beaten in the field and besieged, appealed to Lacedaemon and asked her to help them by invading Attica. Lacedaemon promised, without informing Athens, and intended to do it, but the earthquake prevented her. With it came the secession to Ithome of the Helots and of the Thuriats and Aethaeans of the Perioeci. Most of the Helots were descended from the old Messenians who had been enslaved in the famous war, and so all of them came to be called Messenians. The Lacedaemonians were thus engaged in a war with the rebels in Ithome. In the third year of the siege the Thasians obtained terms from the Athenians: they razed their walls, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay at once the money demanded and tribute in future. They also gave up their possessions on the continent together with the mine.

In the meantime the Lacedaemonians found that the war against the rebels in Ithome was likely to last. They called on their allies for help, and especially on the Athenians, who came in some force under the command of Cimon. They summoned the Athenians so urgently because of their reputed skill in siege operations. A long siege had taught the Lacedaemonians that they themselves lacked this art; otherwise they would have taken the place by assault. This expedition gave rise to the first open quarrel between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians. Assault had failed to take the place, and the Lacedaemonians became apprehensive of the enterprising and revolutionary character of the Athenians. They also regarded them as of alien extraction, and began to fear that if the Athenians stayed, the besieged in Ithome might tempt them to attempt some political changes. So they dismissed them alone of the allies. They did not declare their suspicions, but merely said that they had no further need of them. The Athenians, however, realized that their dismissal did not come from the more honorable of the two possible reasons, but from suspicions that had been formed. They went away deeply offended, conscious that they had done nothing to deserve such treatment from the Lacedaemonians. The instant they returned home they broke off the alliance that had been made against the Mede and allied themselves with Sparta’s enemy Argos; each of the contracting parties took the same oaths, and made the same alliance with the Thessalians.

Meanwhile the rebels in Ithome could no longer prolong their resistance, which had lasted ten years, and surrendered to Lacedaemon. The conditions were that they should leave Peloponnese under safe conduct and never set foot in it again; anyone found there afterward was to be the slave of his captor. It must be known that the Lacedaemonians had an old oracle from Delphi, telling them to let go the suppliant of Zeus at Ithome. So the rebels went out with their children and wives. Athens, hating the Lacedaemonians as she now did, received them and settled them at Naupactus, which she had lately taken from the Ozolian Locrians. The Athenians gained another addition to their confederacy in the Megarians. These left the Lacedaemonian alliance because they were annoyed at a war about boundaries that Corinth had forced on them. The Athenians occupied Megara and Pegae, and built the Megarians their long walls from the city to Nisaea, where they placed an Athenian garrison. This was the principal reason why the Corinthians conceived such a deadly hatred against Athens.

Meanwhile Inaros, son of Psammetichus, was a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian border, with his headquarters at Marea, the town above Pharos. He brought about a revolt of almost the whole of Egypt from King Artaxerxes, placed himself at its head, and invited the Athenians to help him. They were at that moment engaged in an expedition to Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and their allies; they abandoned it and arrived in Egypt. They sailed from the sea into the Nile and made themselves masters of the river and of two-thirds of Memphis. Then they set about attacking the remaining third, called White Castle. Inside it were Persians and Medes who had taken refuge there, and Egyptians who had not joined the rebellion.

Meanwhile the Athenians made a landing from their fleet at Haliae, and a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians engaged them; the Corinthians won. Afterward the Athenians fought the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia, and the Athenians won. War then broke out between Aegina and Athens. A great battle was fought at sea off Aegina between the Athenians and the Aeginetans, each supported by their allies, and the Athenians won it. They took seventy of the enemy’s ships, landed in the country and began a siege under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus. The Peloponnesians wanted to help the Aeginetans, and threw into Aegina three hundred heavy infantry who had earlier served with the Corinthians and Epidaurians. Meanwhile the Corinthians and their allies occupied the heights of Geraneia and marched down into the Megarid. They believed that, with a large force away in Aegina and Egypt, Athens could not help the Megarians without raising the siege of Aegina. But the Athenians did not move the army from Aegina. They raised a force from the old and young men left in the city, and marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides. The battle with the Corinthians was a draw, and the two armies parted, each believing it had won. The Athenians, however, had if anything rather the better of it, and when the Corinthians left they set up a trophy. The elders in the Corinthian city taunted them, and goaded by this the Corinthians made their preparations and, about twelve days later, came and set up their own trophy as victors. The Athenians sallied out from Megara, cut off the party that was busy erecting the trophy, and engaged and defeated the rest. As the beaten army retreated, a considerable division, hard pressed by its pursuers, mistook the road and dashed into a field on private property. A deep trench ran all round it, and there was no way out. The Athenians knew the place. They hemmed in the front with heavy infantry, placed the light troops round in a circle, and stoned all who had gone in. Corinth suffered a severe blow here. The bulk of her army continued its retreat home.

About this time the Athenians began to build the long walls down to the sea, one toward Phalerum and one toward Piraeus. Meanwhile the Phocians made an expedition against Doris, the old home of the Lacedaemonians, which contained the towns of Boeum, Kitinium, and Erineum. When they had taken one of these towns, the Lacedaemonians came to the aid of the Dorians. Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, led them, commanding for King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, who was still a minor; they brought fifteen hundred heavy infantry of their own and ten thousand of their allies. They compelled the Phocians to give the town back on conditions, and then began their retreat. If they went by sea, across the Crissaean Gulf, the Athenian fleet might stop them. The route across Geraneia seemed scarcely safe, because the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. The pass was difficult and always guarded by the Athenians, and now the Lacedaemonians had information that the Athenians meant to dispute their passage. So they resolved to stay in Boeotia and consider which line of march would be safest. They had another reason as well. A party in Athens, hoping to put an end to democracy and to the building of the Long Walls, had secretly encouraged them. Meanwhile the Athenians marched against them with their whole levy, a thousand Argives, and the respective contingents of the rest of their allies; altogether they were fourteen thousand strong. They marched because they believed the Lacedaemonians were at a loss how to effect their passage, and because they suspected an attempt to overthrow the democracy. Some cavalry from their Thessalian allies also joined the Athenians, but these went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle.

The battle was fought at Tanagra in Boeotia. Both sides lost heavily, and victory went to the Lacedaemonians and their allies. They then entered the Megarid and cut down the fruit trees, and returned home by way of Geraneia and the isthmus. Sixty-two days after the battle the Athenians marched into Boeotia under the command of Myronides. They defeated the Boeotians in battle at Oenophyta and became masters of Boeotia and Phocis. They dismantled the walls of the Tanagraeans, took a hundred of the richest men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls. Next the Aeginetans surrendered to Athens on conditions: they pulled down their walls, gave up their ships, and agreed to pay tribute in future. The Athenians, under Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, sailed round Peloponnese and burned the arsenal of Lacedaemon. They took Chalcis, a town of the Corinthians, and in a descent upon Sicyon they defeated the Sicyonians in battle.

Meanwhile the Athenians in Egypt, with their allies, were still there, and they met with every change of fortune in war. At first the Athenians were masters of Egypt. The King sent a Persian, Megabazus, to Lacedaemon with money, to bribe the Peloponnesians to invade Attica and so draw the Athenians away from Egypt. The matter made no progress and the money was being wasted. So he recalled Megabazus with what remained of it, and sent another Persian, Megabuzus, son of Zopyrus, to Egypt with a large army. Megabuzus came by land and defeated the Egyptians and their allies in a battle. He drove the Hellenes out of Memphis and finally shut them up in the island of Prosopitis, where he besieged them for a year and six months. In the end he drained the canal of its water and diverted it into another channel. This left their ships high and dry and joined most of the island to the mainland, and he marched across on foot and took it. So the enterprise of the Hellenes came to ruin after six years of war. Of all that large host a few made their way through Libya and reached Cyrene safely, but most perished. Thus Egypt returned to its subjection to the King, except for Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, whom they could not capture because of the size of the marsh; the marshmen are also the most warlike of the Egyptians. Inaros, the Libyan king, who alone had brought about the Egyptian revolt, was betrayed, captured, and crucified. Meanwhile a relief squadron of fifty vessels had sailed for Egypt from Athens and the rest of the confederacy. Knowing nothing of what had happened, they put in to shore at the Mendesian mouth of the Nile. The troops attacked them from the land and the Phoenician navy from the sea. Most of the ships were destroyed, and the few that remained escaped by retreat. This was the end of the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt.

Meanwhile Orestes, son of Echecratidas, the Thessalian king, had been exiled from Thessaly, and he persuaded the Athenians to restore him. They took their allies the Boeotians and Phocians with them and marched to Pharsalus in Thessaly. They became masters of the country, but only in the immediate neighborhood of the camp, for they could go no further for fear of the Thessalian cavalry. They failed to take the city or to achieve any of the other aims of their expedition, and returned home with Orestes having accomplished nothing. Not long after this, a thousand Athenians embarked in the vessels that were at Pegae (Pegae, it must be remembered, was now theirs) and sailed along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus. They landed in Sicyon and defeated the Sicyonians who engaged them. Then they immediately took the Achaeans with them, sailed across, and marched against Oeniadae in Acarnania and besieged it. But they did not take it, and returned home.

Three years later a truce for five years was made between the Peloponnesians and Athenians. Free now from war with Hellenes, the Athenians made an expedition to Cyprus under the command of Cimon, with two hundred vessels of their own and their allies. Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, asked for help, and sixty of these ships were detached to Egypt; the rest laid siege to Kitium. The death of Cimon and a scarcity of provisions forced them to withdraw from it. They sailed off Salamis in Cyprus and fought the Phoenicians, Cyprians, and Cilicians by land and sea. They won on both elements and went home, together with the squadron that had returned from Egypt. After this the Lacedaemonians marched out on a sacred war. They became masters of the temple at Delphi and put it in the hands of the Delphians. As soon as they had retreated, the Athenians marched out, became masters of the temple, and placed it in the hands of the Phocians.

Some time after this, Boeotian exiles held Orchomenus, Chaeronea, and some other places in Boeotia. The Athenians marched against these hostile places with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and the allied contingents, under the command of Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus. They took Chaeronea and made slaves of the inhabitants, and then began their return, leaving a garrison behind. On the road, the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus attacked them at Coronea, together with some Locrians, Euboean exiles, and others who thought as they did. The Athenians were defeated in battle; some were killed and others taken captive. By a treaty providing for the recovery of the men, the Athenians evacuated all Boeotia; the exiled Boeotians returned, and with all the rest regained their independence.

Soon afterward Euboea revolted from Athens. Pericles had already crossed to the island with an army of Athenians when news was brought him that Megara had revolted, that the Peloponnesians were about to invade Attica, and that the Megarians had cut off the Athenian garrison; only a few had escaped, taking refuge in Nisaea. Before they revolted, the Megarians had let the Corinthians, Sicyonians, and Epidaurians into the town. Pericles meanwhile brought his army back from Euboea in all haste. After this the Peloponnesians marched into Attica as far as Eleusis and Thrius, ravaging the country under the leadership of King Pleistoanax, the son of Pausanias, and went home without advancing further. The Athenians then crossed again to Euboea under the command of Pericles and subdued the whole island. They settled everything but Histiaea by agreement; the Histiaeans they drove out of their homes and occupied their territory themselves.

Not long after their return from Euboea, they made a thirty years’ truce with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, and gave up the posts they held in Peloponnese — Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia. In the sixth year of the truce, war broke out between the Samians and Milesians over Priene. The Milesians had the worse of it and came to Athens to complain loudly against the Samians. Some private persons from Samos itself, who wanted to revolutionize the government, joined them. So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships and set up a democracy. They took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages and lodged them in Lemnos; then they left a garrison in the island and returned home. But some of the Samians had not stayed in the island and had fled to the continent. They came to an agreement with the most powerful men in the city and made an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, who was then satrap of Sardis. They collected a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos by night. First they rose against the commons and secured most of them; next they stole their hostages from Lemnos. After that they revolted, handed over to Pissuthnes the Athenian garrison left with them, together with its commanders, and at once prepared an expedition against Miletus. The Byzantines revolted with them.

The Athenians heard the news and at once sailed against Samos with sixty ships. Sixteen of these never engaged: some went to Caria to watch for the Phoenician fleet, and others to Chios and Lesbos with orders for reinforcements. But forty-four ships under Pericles and nine colleagues gave battle off the island of Tragia to seventy Samian vessels, twenty of them transports, which were sailing from Miletus. The Athenians won. Later they were reinforced by forty ships from Athens and twenty-five Chian and Lesbian vessels. They landed, and since they were stronger on land they surrounded the city with three walls; it was also blockaded from the sea. Meanwhile word came that the Phoenician fleet was approaching to help the Samians; indeed Stesagoras and others had left the island with five ships to bring it. So Pericles took sixty ships from the blockading squadron and left in haste for Caunus and Caria. In the meantime the Samians made a sudden sally and fell on the camp, which they found unfortified. They destroyed the look-out vessels and engaged and defeated those that were launched to meet them. For fourteen days they were masters of their own seas and brought in and carried out what they pleased. But when Pericles arrived, they were shut up again. Fresh reinforcements then came — forty ships from Athens with Thucydides, Hagnon, and Phormio; twenty with Tlepolemus and Anticles; and thirty vessels from Chios and Lesbos. The Samians made a brief attempt at fighting, but could not hold out. After a siege of nine months they surrendered on conditions: they razed their walls, gave hostages, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay the expenses of the war by installments. The Byzantines also agreed to be subject as before.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — Second Congress at Lacedaemon—Preparations for War and Diplomatic Skirmishes—Cylon—Pausanias—Themistocles
paragraphs: Not many years after this, we come at last to the events already related: the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the incidents that served as a pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes, against each other and against the barbarian, took place in the fifty years between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of this war. In that time the Athenians put their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians saw it clearly, yet opposed it only briefly and for the most part stayed inactive. They were slow by long habit to go to war unless necessity forced them, and in this case they were also hampered by wars at home. At last the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy came under its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer. The time had come to throw themselves heart and soul upon the hostile power and break it, if they could, by beginning the present war. They had already made up their own minds that the treaty had been broken and that the Athenians were guilty. Even so, they sent to Delphi and asked the God whether war would be well for them. As it is reported, he answered that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and he promised that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or uninvoked. Still, they wished to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether it was proper to make war. The ambassadors of the confederates arrived and a congress was convened. All spoke their minds, and most of them denounced the Athenians and demanded that the war begin. The Corinthians did so in particular. Earlier they had gone through the cities one by one on their own account, urging them to vote for war, for fear that it would come too late to save Potidæa. They were present on this occasion too, and they came forward last and spoke as follows:

“Fellow allies, we can no longer accuse the Lacedaemonians of failing in their duty. They have not only voted for war themselves, but have gathered us here for that purpose. We say their duty, because supremacy has its duties. Leaders must administer private interests fairly, but they must also show special care for the common welfare, in return for the special honors that all pay them in other ways. As for ourselves, those who have already had dealings with the Athenians need no warning to be on their guard against them. The states farther inland, away from the main routes of communication, should understand that if they fail to support the coast powers, they will damage the passage of their own produce down to the sea for export, and the reception in exchange of imports from the sea. They must not judge what is said here carelessly, as if it did not concern them. They must expect that if the coast powers are sacrificed, the danger will one day reach the interior too, and they must recognize that their own interests are deeply involved in this discussion. For these reasons they should not hesitate to exchange peace for war. Wise men stay quiet as long as they are not injured, but brave men leave peace for war when they are injured, and return to an understanding when a favorable opportunity comes. They are neither intoxicated by success in war nor willing to take an injury for the sake of the pleasant tranquillity of peace. Indeed, if you stay inactive, to hesitate for the sake of such pleasures is the quickest way to lose the sweets of repose to which you cling. And to conceive extravagant pretensions from success in war is to forget how hollow is the confidence that elates you. Many ill-conceived plans have succeeded because their opponents were still more foolish, but many more that seemed well laid have ended in disgrace. The confidence with which we form our schemes is never fully justified in their execution. Speculation is carried on in safety, but when it comes to action, fear causes failure.

“To apply these rules to ourselves: if we are kindling war now, we do so under the pressure of injury and with adequate grounds of complaint, and when we have chastised the Athenians we will stop in due season. We have many reasons to expect success. First, we are superior in numbers and in military experience. Second, we are generally and unfailingly obedient in carrying out orders. As for naval strength, which they possess, we shall build it up from the resources each of us already has and from the moneys at Olympia and Delphi. A loan from these will enable us to lure away their foreign sailors by offering higher pay. For the power of Athens is bought rather than national, while ours will not run the same risk, since its strength lies more in men than in money. A single defeat at sea will in all likelihood ruin them. If they hold out, we shall have the more time to train ourselves in naval matters, and as soon as we have reached equality in skill, we need hardly ask whether we shall be their superiors in courage. For the advantages we have by nature they cannot acquire by education, while their superiority in skill we can remove by practice. The money required for these purposes shall be provided by our contributions. Nothing could be more monstrous than to suggest that, while their allies never tire of contributing toward their own servitude, we should refuse to spend on vengeance and self-preservation the treasure that, by refusing, we shall lose to Athenian rapacity and see used for our own ruin.

“We have other ways of carrying on the war as well: the revolt of their allies, which is the surest way of depriving them of the revenues that are the source of their strength; the establishment of fortified positions in their country; and various operations that cannot be foreseen at present. For of all things war proceeds least by definite rules. It draws mainly on itself for devices to meet an emergency, and in such cases the party that faces the struggle and keeps his temper best finds the most security, while the one who loses his temper finds corresponding disaster. Let us also reflect that if this were merely a series of territorial disputes between rival neighbors, it might be borne. But in Athens we have an enemy that is a match for our whole coalition and more than a match for any one of its members. Unless we make a united stand against her, as a body and as individual nations and cities, she will easily conquer us when we are divided and take us one by one. That conquest, terrible as it may sound, would, it must be understood, have no other end than slavery pure and simple. Peloponnese cannot even hear that word whispered without disgrace, nor see so many states abused by one without disgrace. Meanwhile people would conclude either that we were justly treated so, or that we put up with it out of cowardice and were proving ourselves degenerate sons, since we would not even secure for ourselves the freedom that our fathers gave to Hellas. We would be allowing a tyrant state to be established in Hellas, though in individual states we think it our duty to put down sole rulers. We do not know how this conduct can be held free from three of the gravest failings: want of sense, want of courage, or want of vigilance. For we do not suppose that you have taken refuge in that contempt of an enemy which has proved so fatal in so many instances, a feeling which has ruined so many that it has come to be called not contemptuous but contemptible.

“There is, however, no advantage in reflecting on the past beyond what may serve the present. For the future we must provide by holding on to what the present gives us and redoubling our efforts. It is hereditary with us to win virtue as the fruit of labor, and you must not change the habit, even if you now have a slight advantage in wealth and resources. For it is not right that what was won in want should be lost in plenty. No, we must advance boldly to the war, for many reasons. The god has commanded it and promised to be with us, and the rest of Hellas will join the struggle, some from fear, some from interest. You will not be the first to break a treaty, since the god, in advising us to go to war, judges it to be violated already. Rather you will be supporting a treaty that has been outraged. Indeed, treaties are broken not by resistance but by aggression.

“Your position, therefore, from whatever side you view it, will amply justify you in going to war. We recommend this step in the interests of all, bearing in mind that identity of interest is the surest of bonds, whether between states or between individuals. Do not delay, then, to help Potidæa, a Dorian city besieged by Ionians, which is quite a reversal of the proper order of things, nor to assert the freedom of the rest. We cannot wait any longer when waiting can only mean immediate disaster for some of us, and, if it becomes known that we have conferred but do not venture to protect ourselves, like disaster in the near future for the rest. Do not delay, fellow allies. Be convinced of the necessity of the crisis and the wisdom of this counsel, and vote for the war. Do not be deterred by its immediate terrors, but look beyond them to the lasting peace that will follow. Out of war peace gains fresh stability, but refusing to leave repose for war is not so sure a way of avoiding danger. We must believe that the tyrant city established in Hellas has been established against all alike, with a program of universal empire, part fulfilled and part in contemplation. Let us then attack and reduce it, and win future security for ourselves and freedom for the Hellenes who are now enslaved.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. The Lacedaemonians had now heard all the opinions. They took the vote of all the allied states present in order, great and small alike, and the majority voted for war. This was decided, but it was still impossible for them to begin at once, since they were unprepared. It was resolved that the different states should procure the means required, and that there should be no delay. And indeed, despite the time taken up by the necessary arrangements, less than a year passed before Attica was invaded and the war openly begun.

This interval was spent in sending embassies to Athens with complaints, in order to have as good a pretext for war as possible if she paid no attention to them. The first Lacedaemonian embassy ordered the Athenians to drive out the curse of the goddess. Its history is as follows. In former generations there was an Athenian named Cylon, a victor at the Olympic games, of good birth and powerful position, who had married a daughter of Theagenes, a Megarian who was then tyrant of Megara. Now Cylon was consulting the oracle at Delphi, and the god told him to seize the Acropolis of Athens on the grand festival of Zeus. So he obtained a force from Theagenes and persuaded his friends to join him. When the Olympic festival in Peloponnese came, he seized the Acropolis, intending to make himself tyrant. He thought this was the grand festival of Zeus, and also an occasion fitting for an Olympic victor. Whether the grand festival that was meant was in Attica or elsewhere, he never considered, and the oracle did not offer to settle. For the Athenians also have a festival called the grand festival of Zeus Meilichios or Gracious, namely the Diasia. It is celebrated outside the city, and the whole people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the country. However, believing he had chosen the right time, he made the attempt. As soon as the Athenians noticed it, they flocked in from the country, one and all, sat down, and laid siege to the citadel. But as time went on, most of them grew weary of the labor of the blockade and departed. The responsibility of keeping guard was left to the nine archons, with full powers to arrange everything as they judged best. It must be known that at that time most political functions were discharged by the nine archons. Meanwhile Cylon and his besieged companions were suffering from want of food and water. Cylon and his brother made their escape, but the rest were hard pressed, and some were even dying of famine, so they seated themselves as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis. The Athenians who had been charged with keeping guard saw them at the point of death in the temple. They raised them up on the understanding that no harm should be done to them, led them out, and killed them. Some who took refuge at the altars of the awful goddesses as they passed by were dispatched on the spot. For this deed the men who killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess, they and their descendants. So these accursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, and driven out again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction. The living were driven out, and the bones of the dead were taken up, and thus they were cast out. For all that, they came back afterwards, and their descendants are still in the city.

This, then, was the curse that the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out. As they pretended, they were motivated chiefly by concern for the honor of the gods. But they also knew that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side, and they thought that his banishment would greatly advance their designs on Athens. They did not really hope to bring this about. They thought rather to create a prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen, who would feel that the war was partly caused by his misfortune. For he was the most powerful man of his time and the leading Athenian statesman. He opposed the Lacedaemonians in everything, would allow no concessions, and constantly urged the Athenians on to war.

The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of Taenarus. The Lacedaemonians had once raised some Helot suppliants up from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away and killed them, and they believe the great earthquake at Sparta to have been a retribution for it. The Athenians also ordered them to drive out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House. Its history is as follows. Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this was his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted. He was not sent out again in a public capacity, but he took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without the authority of the Lacedaemonians, and arrived in the Hellespont as a private person. He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, but really to carry on his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, since he was ambitious of reigning over Hellas. What first enabled him to put the King under an obligation, and to make a beginning of the whole design, was this. Some connections and kinsmen of the King had been taken in Byzantium when it was captured from the Medes, during his first stay there, after the return from Cyprus. He sent these captives off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, giving out that they had escaped from him. He managed this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had put in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners. He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which, as was discovered afterwards, were as follows: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, wishing to do you a favor, sends you these prisoners of war. I also propose, with your approval, to marry your daughter, and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. I may say that I think I am able to do this, with your co-operation. So if any of this pleases you, send a trustworthy man to the sea, through whom we may conduct our correspondence in future.”

This was all that the writing revealed, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter. He sent Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea, with orders to replace Megabates, the previous governor in the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send over to Pausanias at Byzantium as quickly as possible a letter that he entrusted to him. Artabazus was to show Pausanias the royal signet, and to carry out with all care and fidelity any commission he might receive from Pausanias on the King’s business. When Artabazus arrived, he carried out the King’s orders and sent over the letter, which contained the following answer: “Thus says King Xerxes to Pausanias. For the men whom you have saved for me across the sea from Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded for ever, and I am well pleased with your proposals. Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing any of your promises to me. Do not let them be hindered by the cost of gold or silver, nor by the number of troops, wherever their presence may be needed. With Artabazus, an honorable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, in whatever way may be most to the honor and interest of us both.”

Pausanias had earlier been held in high honor by the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea. After he received this letter he became prouder than ever and could no longer live in the usual style. He left Byzantium in a Median dress and was attended on his march through Thrace by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians. He kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to hide his intentions, but betrayed in trifles what his ambition one day meant to enact on a grander scale. He also made himself hard to approach and showed such a violent temper to everyone without exception that no one could come near him. Indeed, this was the principal reason why the confederacy went over to the Athenians.

When this conduct came to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, it caused his first recall. After his second voyage out in the ship of Hermione, without their orders, he gave proofs of similar behavior. He was besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the Athenians, and did not return to Sparta. News came that he had settled at Colonae in the Troad and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good purpose. The ephors, no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy. He was anxious above everything to avoid suspicion, and confident that he could quash the charge with money, so he returned to Sparta a second time. At first the ephors threw him into prison (their powers enable them to do this to the King). Soon he settled the matter and came out again, and offered himself for trial to anyone who wished to bring an inquiry against him.

Now the Spartans, whether his enemies or the nation at large, had no tangible proof against him, of the indubitable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family who was at that moment in high office. He was regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus, Leonidas’s son, who was still a minor. But his contempt for the laws and his imitation of the barbarians gave grounds for much suspicion that he was discontented with the established order. They reviewed all the occasions on which he had in any way departed from the regular customs, and remembered that he had taken it upon himself to have the following couplet inscribed on the tripod at Delphi, which was dedicated by the Hellenes as the first-fruits of the spoil of the Medes:
The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised This monument, that Phœbus might be praised.

At the time the Lacedaemonians had at once erased the couplet and inscribed the names of the cities that had helped overthrow the barbarian and had dedicated the offering. Yet it was considered that Pausanias had been guilty of a grave offense here, and in the light of the attitude he had since taken, it gained a new significance and seemed quite in keeping with his present schemes. Besides, they were informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots. Such indeed was the fact, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in insurrection and help him carry out his plans to the end. Even now the ephors mistrusted the evidence even of the Helots themselves and would not consent to take any decided step against him. They were following their regular custom toward themselves, which is to be slow in taking any irrevocable resolve concerning a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof. At last, it is said, the man who was going to carry the last letter for the King to Artabazus turned informer. He was a man of Argilus, once the favorite and most trusted servant of Pausanias. He was alarmed by the reflection that none of the previous messengers had ever returned. So he counterfeited the seal, in order that, if he found himself mistaken in his surmises, or if Pausanias should ask to make some correction, he would not be discovered. Then he undid the letter and found the postscript he had suspected, namely an order to put him to death.

The ephors were shown the letter and now felt more certain. Still, they wished to hear Pausanias commit himself with their own ears. So the man went by appointment to Taenarus as a suppliant, and there built himself a hut divided in two by a partition. Inside it he concealed some of the ephors and let them hear the whole matter plainly. For Pausanias came to him and asked the reason for his position as a suppliant. The man reproached him with the order that he had written concerning him, and declared one by one all the other circumstances: how he had never yet brought Pausanias into any danger while employed as agent between him and the King, and yet, like the mass of his servants, was to be rewarded with death. Pausanias admitted all this, told him not to be angry about it, gave him a pledge of raising him up from the temple, and begged him to set off as quickly as possible and not to hinder the business in hand.

The ephors listened carefully and then departed. They took no action for the moment, but, having at last attained certainty, were preparing to arrest him in the city. It is reported that as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors what he was coming for. Another, too, made him a secret signal and betrayed it to him out of kindness. He set off running for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, whose enclosure was near at hand, and took sanctuary before they could seize him. He entered a small chamber that formed part of the temple, to avoid being exposed to the weather, and lay still there. The ephors, for the moment outdistanced in the pursuit, afterwards took the roof off the chamber, made sure that he was inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and stayed before the place, reducing him by starvation. When they found that he was on the point of expiring, just as he was in the chamber, they brought him out of the temple while the breath was still in him, and as soon as he was brought out he died. They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they cast criminals, but finally decided to bury him somewhere nearby. But the god at Delphi afterwards ordered the Lacedaemonians to move the tomb to the place of his death, where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares. Since what had been done was a curse upon them, he also ordered them to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House. So they had two brazen statues made and dedicated them as a substitute for Pausanias. The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians to drive out what the god himself had pronounced to be a curse.

To return to the Medism of Pausanias. In the course of the inquiry, material was found that implicated Themistocles, and the Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians and required them to punish him as they had punished Pausanias. The Athenians consented to do so. But he had, as it happened, been ostracized, and, while living at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of Peloponnese. So they sent persons with instructions to take him wherever they found him, accompanied by the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join in the pursuit. But Themistocles got wind of their intentions and fled from Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations to him. But the Corcyraeans said they could not venture to shelter him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the mainland opposite. The officers who hung on the reports of his movements pursued him, and at a loss where to turn, he was compelled to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms. Admetus happened not to be indoors, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth. Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was.
