Having, as they considered, suffered evil at the hands of the Plataeans, they brought them in again one by one and asked each of them the same question, that is, whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and allies any service in the war. When a man said that he had not, they took him out and slew him, without exception. The Plataeans thus massacred numbered not less than two hundred, together with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The Thebans gave the city for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit. Afterward they razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Next to the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches, which they dedicated to Hera, and for her they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten years’ lease to Theban occupiers. The Lacedaemonians’ adverse attitude in the whole Plataean affair was adopted mainly to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.

Meanwhile the forty ships of the Peloponnesians that had gone to the relief of the Lesbians, and that we left fleeing across the open sea with the Athenians in pursuit, were caught in a storm off Crete. They scattered from there and made their way to Peloponnese. At Cyllene they found thirteen Leucadian and Ambraciot galleys, with Brasidas, son of Tellis, who had lately arrived as counsellor to Alcidas. The Lacedaemonians, now that the Lesbian expedition had failed, had resolved to strengthen their fleet and sail to Corcyra, where a revolution had broken out. They meant to arrive before the twelve Athenian ships at Naupactus could be reinforced from Athens. Brasidas and Alcidas began to prepare accordingly.

The Corcyraean revolution began with the return of the prisoners taken in the sea-fights off Epidamnus. The Corinthians had released them, nominally on the security of eight hundred talents given by their proxeni, but in reality on their engagement to bring Corcyra over to Corinth. These men set about canvassing each of the citizens and intriguing to detach the city from Athens. An Athenian and a Corinthian vessel arrived with envoys on board, and a conference was held, in which the Corcyraeans voted to remain allies of the Athenians according to their agreement, but to be friends of the Peloponnesians as they had been formerly. Meanwhile the returned prisoners brought to trial Peithias, a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and leader of the commons, on the charge of enslaving Corcyra to Athens. He was acquitted, and in retaliation accused five of the richest of their number of cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous, the legal penalty being a stater for each stake. They were convicted, and since the amount of the penalty was very large, they seated themselves as suppliants in the temples, to be allowed to pay it by installments. But Peithias, who was a member of the senate, prevailed on that body to enforce the law. The accused were rendered desperate by the law, and they also learned that Peithias intended, while still a member of the senate, to persuade the people to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with Athens. They banded together, armed with daggers, burst suddenly into the senate, and killed Peithias and sixty others, senators and private persons. Only a few of the party of Peithias took refuge in the Athenian galley, which had not yet departed.

After this outrage, the conspirators called the Corcyraeans to an assembly. They said that this would turn out for the best and would save them from being enslaved by Athens. For the future, they proposed to receive neither party unless it came peacefully in a single ship, and to treat any larger number as enemies. Having made this motion, they forced the assembly to adopt it, and at once sent envoys to Athens to justify what had been done and to dissuade the refugees there from any hostile move that might bring on a reaction.

When the embassy arrived, the Athenians arrested the envoys and all who had listened to them, as revolutionists, and lodged them in Aegina. Meanwhile a Corinthian galley arrived on the island with Lacedaemonian envoys, and the dominant Corcyraean party attacked the commons and defeated them in battle. When night came on, the commons took refuge in the Acropolis and the higher parts of the city and gathered there. They also held the Hyllaic harbor. Their adversaries occupied the market-place, where most of them lived, and the harbor next to it, which looks toward the mainland.

Nothing of importance happened the next day except skirmishes. Each party sent into the country to offer freedom to the slaves and to invite them to join it. The mass of the slaves answered the appeal of the commons, and their antagonists received reinforcements of eight hundred mercenaries from the continent.

After a day’s interval, fighting began again. The commons won, since they had the advantage in numbers and position, and the women also helped them bravely, pelting the enemy with tiles from the houses and standing up to the melee with a fortitude beyond their sex. Toward dusk the oligarchs were in full rout. They feared that the victorious commons might assault and take the arsenal and put them to the sword, so they set fire to the houses around the marketplace and to the lodging-houses, to bar the commons’ advance. They spared neither their own houses nor those of their neighbors. Much of the merchants’ stock was burned, and the city risked total destruction, if a wind had come to help the flames by blowing on them. Fighting now stopped, and both sides kept quiet and spent the night on guard. The Corinthian ship, after the victory of the commons, stole out to sea, and most of the mercenaries secretly crossed over to the continent.

The next day the Athenian general Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian heavy infantry. He at once tried to bring about a settlement. He persuaded the two parties to agree to bring ten of the ringleaders to trial (these presently fled), while the rest were to live in peace, make terms with each other, and enter into a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians. This arranged, he was about to sail away, when the leaders of the commons induced him to leave them five of his ships, to make their adversaries less inclined to make a move, while they would man an equal number of their own and send them with him. He had no sooner consented than they began to enroll their enemies for the ships. These men, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, sat down as suppliants in the temple of the Dioscuri. Nicostratus tried to reassure them and to persuade them to rise, but without success. The commons then armed themselves on this pretext. They alleged that the refusal of their adversaries to sail with them proved the hollowness of their intentions, and they took their arms out of their houses. They would have killed some of those they fell in with, if Nicostratus had not prevented it. The rest of the party saw what was going on and sat down as suppliants in the temple of Hera, being not less than four hundred in number. The commons then feared that these men might take some desperate decision, and induced them to rise. They conveyed them over to the island in front of the temple, where provisions were sent across to them.

At this stage in the revolution, the fourth or fifth day after the men had been moved to the island, the Peloponnesian ships came in from Cyllene, where they had been stationed since returning from Ionia. They numbered fifty-three and were still commanded by Alcidas, though Brasidas was also on board as his adviser. They anchored at Sybota, a harbor on the mainland, and at daybreak sailed for Corcyra.

The Corcyraeans were in great confusion and alarm at the state of things in the city and at the approach of the invader. They at once began to equip sixty vessels, and sent them out against the enemy as fast as they were manned, although the Athenians recommended that the Corcyraeans let the Athenians sail out first and follow themselves afterward with all their ships together. When the Corcyraean vessels came up to the enemy in this straggling fashion, two immediately deserted. In others the crews were fighting among themselves, and there was no order in anything that was done. So the Peloponnesians, seeing their confusion, placed twenty ships against the Corcyraeans and ranged the rest against the twelve Athenian ships, among which were the two vessels Salaminia and Paralus.

The Corcyraeans attacked without judgment and in small detachments, and were already crippled by their own misconduct. The Athenians were afraid of the enemy’s numbers and of being surrounded, so they did not venture to attack the main body or even the center of the division opposed to them. They fell upon its wing and sank one vessel. After that the Peloponnesians formed in a circle, and the Athenians rowed round them and tried to throw them into disorder. The division opposed to the Corcyraeans saw this and, fearing a repetition of the disaster at Naupactus, came to support their friends. The whole fleet now bore down together upon the Athenians, who retired before it, backing water. They retired as leisurely as possible, in order to give the Corcyraeans time to escape while the enemy was kept occupied in this way. Such was the character of this sea-fight, which lasted until sunset.

The Corcyraeans now feared that the enemy would press home their victory, sail against the town and rescue the men on the island, or strike some other equally decisive blow. So they carried the men back to the temple of Hera and put a guard on the city. The Peloponnesians had won the sea-fight, yet they did not venture to attack the town. They took the thirteen Corcyraean vessels they had captured and sailed back to the continent, the point from which they had set out. The next day they again held back from the city, although the disorder and panic were at their height, and although Brasidas, it is said, pressed Alcidas, who outranked him, to attack. Instead they landed on the promontory of Leukimme and laid waste the country.

Meanwhile the commons in Corcyra were still in great fear that the fleet would attack them. To save the town, they came to a parley with the suppliants and their friends, and prevailed upon some of them to go on board the ships, of which they still manned thirty, against the expected attack. But the Peloponnesians, after ravaging the country until midday, sailed away. Toward nightfall beacon signals informed them that sixty Athenian vessels were approaching from Leucas, under the command of Eurymedon, son of Thucles. The Athenians had sent this fleet off on hearing of the revolution and of the fleet with Alcidas being about to sail for Corcyra.

The Peloponnesians therefore set off at once in haste by night for home, coasting along the shore. They hauled their ships across the Isthmus of Leucas, in order not to be seen doubling it, and so departed. The Corcyraeans learned that the Athenian fleet was approaching and the enemy had left. They brought the Messenians from outside the walls into the town and ordered the fleet they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbor. While it was doing so, they killed such of their enemies as they laid hands on, and afterward, as they landed them, they dispatched those whom they had persuaded to go on board the ships. Next they went to the sanctuary of Hera and persuaded about fifty men to take their trial, and condemned them all to death. The mass of the suppliants who had refused to do so saw what was happening and killed each other there in the consecrated ground. Some hanged themselves on the trees, and others destroyed themselves as each was able. For seven days Eurymedon stayed with his sixty ships, and during that time the Corcyraeans were busy butchering those of their fellow citizens whom they regarded as their enemies. The crime charged was that of trying to put down the democracy, but some were killed also out of private hatred, and others by their debtors because of the money they owed. Death raged in every shape. As usually happens at such times, there was no length to which violence did not go. Sons were killed by their fathers, and suppliants were dragged from the altar or killed upon it. Some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there.

The revolution was so bloody in its course, and made the greater impression because it was one of the first to occur. Later, one may say, the whole Hellenic world was convulsed. In every place the popular chiefs struggled to bring in the Athenians, and the oligarchs to bring in the Lacedaemonians. In peace there would have been neither pretext nor desire to invite them. But in war either faction could always call on an alliance, to hurt its adversaries and to its own corresponding advantage, and so the revolutionary parties never lacked opportunities to bring in the foreigner. The sufferings that revolution brought on the cities were many and terrible. They have happened and always will happen, as long as human nature remains the same, though they are more severe or milder, and take different forms, according to the particular circumstances. In peace and prosperity, states and individuals hold better sentiments, because they are not suddenly confronted with imperious necessities. War, however, takes away the easy supply of daily wants, and so is a rough master, that brings most men’s characters down to the level of their fortunes. Revolution thus ran its course from city to city. The places it reached last had heard what had been done before, and went still further in refining their inventions, both in the cunning of their enterprises and in the atrocity of their reprisals. Words had to change their ordinary meaning and take the meaning now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation was held to be a cloak for unmanliness; the ability to see all sides of a question, an inability to act on any. Frantic violence became the mark of manliness; cautious plotting, a justifiable means of self-defense. The man who proposed extreme measures was always trusted; his opponent was suspected. To succeed in a plot was to have a shrewd head, and to detect one was to be shrewder still. But to try to make sure that you would have to do neither was to break up your party and to be afraid of your adversaries. In short, applause went equally to the man who struck first at one intending a crime and to the man who put the idea of a crime into the head of one who had never thought of it. In the end even blood became a weaker tie than party, because those bound by party were readier to dare everything without reserve. Such associations did not look to the blessings of established institutions; they were formed by ambition to overthrow them. Their members trusted each other less because of any religious sanction than because they shared in crime. The fair proposals of an adversary were met by the stronger side with jealous precautions, not with generous confidence. Revenge was also valued above self-preservation. Oaths of reconciliation were offered on either side only to meet an immediate difficulty, and held good only while no other weapon was at hand. When an opportunity came, the man who first dared to seize it, and caught his enemy off his guard, found this perfidious vengeance sweeter than an open one. Safety aside, success by treachery also won him the prize of superior intelligence. Indeed men generally find it easier to call rogues clever than simpletons honest, and are as ashamed of being the second as they are proud of being the first. The cause of all these evils was the lust for power that sprang from greed and ambition, and from these passions came the violence of parties once they were engaged in contention. The leaders in the cities each had the fairest professions: on the one side the cry of political equality for the people, on the other of a moderate aristocracy. They sought prizes for themselves in the public interests they pretended to cherish. They recoiled from no means in their struggles for ascendancy, and engaged in the direst excesses. In their acts of vengeance they went further still. They did not stop at what justice or the good of the state demanded, but made the party caprice of the moment their only standard. They were as ready to invoke the condemnation of an unjust verdict as the authority of the strong arm, to glut the animosities of the hour. Thus religion was in honor with neither party, but the use of fair phrases to arrive at guilty ends was in high reputation. Meanwhile the moderate part of the citizens perished between the two, either because they did not join in the quarrel, or because envy would not suffer them to escape.

In this way every form of iniquity took root in the Hellenic countries as a result of the troubles. The ancient simplicity, in which honor had so large a part, was laughed down and disappeared. Society became divided into camps, and in them no man trusted his fellow. There was no promise that could be depended on to end this, and no oath that could command respect. All parties rather dwelt in their calculations on the hopelessness of any permanent state of things, and were more concerned with self-defense than capable of confidence. In this contest the blunter wits were most successful. They were apprehensive of their own deficiencies and of the cleverness of their antagonists. They feared to be worsted in debate and to be surprised by the combinations of their more versatile opponents, and so they boldly turned to action at once. Their adversaries, meanwhile, arrogantly thought that they would know in time, and that there was no need to secure by action what policy could provide. They often fell victims to their want of precaution.

Meanwhile Corcyra gave the first example of most of the crimes just described. It saw the reprisals taken, when their hour came, by the governed, who had never known equitable treatment from their rulers, only insolence. It saw the iniquitous resolves of those who wished to escape their accustomed poverty and ardently coveted their neighbors’ goods. And it saw the savage and pitiless excesses into which men were carried by their ungovernable passions, men who had entered the struggle in a party spirit and not as a class. Life in the cities was now thrown into confusion. Human nature, which always rebels against the law and was now its master, gladly showed itself ungoverned in passion, above respect for justice, and the enemy of all superiority. For revenge would not have been set above religion, nor gain above justice, had it not been for the fatal power of envy. Indeed, in pursuing their revenge, men too often take it upon themselves to set the example of doing away with those general laws on which all alike can rely for salvation in adversity. They do this instead of letting them stand against the day of danger, when their aid may be needed.

The revolutionary passions had thus shown themselves for the first time in the factions of Corcyra. Then Eurymedon and the Athenian fleet sailed away. After that, some five hundred Corcyraean exiles, who had managed to escape, seized some forts on the mainland. They became masters of the Corcyraean territory across the water and used it as a base to plunder their countrymen on the island, doing so much damage that they caused a severe famine in the town. They also sent envoys to Lacedaemon and Corinth to negotiate their restoration, but had no success. Afterward they collected boats and mercenaries and crossed over to the island, about six hundred in all. They burned their boats, so as to have no hope except in becoming masters of the country, and went up to Mount Istone. There they fortified themselves, began to harass those in the city, and gained command of the country.

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships to Sicily, under Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus. The Syracusans and Leontines were at war there. The Syracusans had as allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina. These cities had been part of the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had taken no active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians sided with the Syracusans, and the Rhegians with their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens, appealing to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin, and asked the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality they wished to stop the export of Sicilian corn to Peloponnese and to test whether Sicily could be brought into subjection. So they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — Year of the War—Campaigns of Demosthenes in Western Greece—Ruin of Ambracia
paragraphs: Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the plague attacked the Athenians a second time. It had never entirely left them, but its ravages had notably abated. This second visit lasted no less than a year, whereas the first had lasted two, and nothing distressed the Athenians and reduced their power more than this. No fewer than four thousand four hundred heavy infantry in the ranks died of it, and three hundred cavalry, besides a number of the common people that was never ascertained. At the same time came the many earthquakes at Athens, in Euboea and in Boeotia, particularly at Orchomenus in Boeotia.

That same winter the Athenians in Sicily, with the Rhegians, sailed against the islands of Aeolus with thirty ships. In summer an invasion was impossible there, because the islands lack water. The Liparaeans, a Cnidian colony, hold them. They live on Lipara, one of the group and not a large island, and from it they farm the others: Didyme, Strongyle and Hiera. The people of those parts believe that Hephaestus has his forge in Hiera, because they see it throw up a great deal of flame by night and smoke by day. The islands lie off the coast of the Sicels and the Messinese, and were allies of the Syracusans. The Athenians ravaged their land. The inhabitants would not submit, and the Athenians sailed back to Rhegium. So the winter ended, and with it the fifth year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.

The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies set out to invade Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus. They went as far as the Isthmus, but there were numerous earthquakes, and they turned back without the invasion taking place. At about the time when these earthquakes were so common, the sea at Orobiae, in Euboea, drew back from the line of coast as it then was, and returned in a huge wave. It flooded a great part of the town and retreated, leaving some of it still under water. So what was once land is now sea, and those of the inhabitants who could not run up to higher ground in time perished. A similar flood occurred at Atalanta, the island off the coast of the Opuntian Locrians. It carried away part of the Athenian fort and wrecked one of two ships that had been drawn up on the beach. At Peparethus the sea also drew back a little, though no flood followed, and an earthquake threw down part of the wall, the town hall and a few other buildings. The cause of this phenomenon, in my opinion, must be sought in the earthquake. Where its shock has been most violent, the sea is driven back and then suddenly recoils with redoubled force, and this causes the flood. Without an earthquake I do not see how such an accident could happen.

During the same summer the different belligerents carried on different operations in Sicily: the Siceliots against each other, and the Athenians and their allies. I shall, however, confine myself to the actions in which the Athenians took part, choosing the most important. The Athenian general Charoeades was killed in battle by the Syracusans, and this left Laches in sole command of the fleet. He now led it, together with the allies, against Mylae, a place belonging to the Messinese. Two Messinese battalions were garrisoned at Mylae, and they laid an ambush for the party landing from the ships. The Athenians and their allies routed them with great slaughter, then assaulted the fortification and forced them to surrender the Acropolis and march with them against Messina. This town also submitted afterwards, when the Athenians and their allies approached, and gave hostages and all the other securities demanded.

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships around Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus. They sent sixty other ships, with two thousand heavy infantry, under Nicias, son of Niceratus, against Melos, wishing to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not win their submission, so the fleet weighed anchor from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry set out at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia. There they were met, at a signal agreed beforehand, by the whole levy from Athens under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped and spent that day ravaging the Tanagraean territory, and stayed there for the night. The next day they defeated those Tanagraeans who sailed out against them, together with some Thebans who had come up to help the Tanagraeans. They took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew, the troops to the city and the others to the ships. Nicias with his sixty ships coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, for the following reason. The Malians form three tribes in all: the Paralians, the Hiereans and the Trachinians. The Trachinians had suffered severely in a war with their neighbors the Oetaeans, and at first intended to give themselves up to Athens. Then they feared that they would not find in her the security they sought, and sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians joined in this embassy with the same request, since they suffered from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians determined to send out the colony. They wished to assist the Trachinians and Dorians, and they also thought that the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet could be made ready there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short passage to the island, and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. They first consulted the god at Delphi and received a favorable answer. Then they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, and invited any others of the Hellenes who wished to go with them, except Ionians, Achaeans and certain other nationalities. Three Lacedaemonians led them as founders of the colony: Leon, Alcidas and Damagon. Once the settlement was made, they fortified the city anew. It is now called Heraclea, and lies about four miles and a half from Thermopylae and two miles and a quarter from the sea. They began building docks, and closed the side toward Thermopylae right at the pass itself, so that the place could be easily defended.

The foundation of this town was evidently meant to annoy Euboea, since the passage across to Cenaeum in that island is a short one. At first it caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, for the town never gave the Athenians any trouble. The reason was as follows. The Thessalians were sovereign in those parts, and their territory was menaced by the foundation of the town. They were afraid that it might prove a very powerful neighbor, and so they continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers, since people flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and therefore thought secure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share toward ruining its prosperity and reducing its population. They frightened away the greater part of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbors to prevail against them.

The same summer, at about the time when the Athenians were detained at Melos, their fellow citizens in the thirty ships cruising around Peloponnese cut off some guards in an ambush at Ellomenus in Leucadia. They then went against Leucas itself with a large armament, having been reinforced by the whole levy of the Acarnanians except Oeniadae, and by the Zacynthians, the Cephallenians and fifteen ships from Corcyra. The Leucadians watched their land being devastated, both outside and inside the isthmus on which the town of Leucas and the temple of Apollo stand, but made no move because of the overwhelming numbers of the enemy. The Acarnanians urged Demosthenes, the Athenian general, to build a wall to cut the town off from the continent. They were convinced that this measure would secure its capture and rid them once and for all of a most troublesome enemy.

Meanwhile the Messenians had persuaded Demosthenes that he had a fine opportunity. With so large an army gathered, he should attack the Aetolians. They were enemies of Naupactus, and reducing them would also make it easy to bring the rest of that part of the continent over to Athens. The Aetolians were a numerous and warlike nation, but they lived in unwalled villages far apart from one another and had only light armor. The Messenians said they could be subdued without much difficulty before any help could reach them. They recommended attacking the Apodotians first, then the Ophionians, and after them the Eurytanians. These are the largest tribe in Aetolia; their language is said to be exceedingly hard to understand, and they eat their meat raw. When these were subdued, the rest would easily submit.

Demosthenes consented to this plan, not only to please the Messenians, but also in the belief that by adding the Aetolians to his other continental allies he would be able to march against the Boeotians without aid from home. He would go by way of Ozolian Locris to Kytinium in Doris, keeping Parnassus on his right until he descended to the Phocians. These he could force to join him if their ancient friendship for Athens did not, as he expected, decide them at once. Once in Phocis he would already be on the frontier of Boeotia. He therefore weighed anchor from Leucas, against the wish of the Acarnanians, and sailed with his whole armament along the coast to Sollium, where he told them his intention. They refused to agree to it because Leucas was not being besieged, so he started on his expedition against the Aetolians with the rest of the forces: the Cephallenians, the Messenians and the Zacynthians, and three hundred Athenian marines from his own ships (the fifteen Corcyraean vessels had departed). He established his base at Oeneon in Locris, since the Ozolian Locrians were allies of Athens and were to meet him with all their forces in the interior. They were neighbors of the Aetolians and armed in the same way, and it was thought that their knowledge of the country and of the enemy’s manner of fighting would make them of great service on the expedition.

Demosthenes bivouacked with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in accordance with an oracle that had foretold he would die in Nemea. At daybreak he set out to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris. He had determined to pursue his conquests as far as the Ophionians, and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had known of his design from the moment it was formed. As soon as the army invaded their country, they came up in great force with all their tribes. Even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians and the Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The Messenians, however, stood by their original advice. They assured Demosthenes that the Aetolians were an easy conquest. He should press on as fast as he could, they said, and try to take each village as he came to it, instead of waiting until the whole nation was under arms against him. His advisers led him on, and he trusted in his fortune, since nobody had opposed him so far. He did not wait for the Locrian reinforcements, who were to have supplied the light-armed darters he lacked most. He advanced and stormed Aegitium. Its inhabitants fled before him and took positions on the hills above the town, which stood on high ground about nine miles from the sea. By now the Aetolians had gathered to the rescue. They attacked the Athenians and their allies, running down from the hills on every side and hurling javelins. When the Athenian army advanced they fell back, and when it retired they came on. For a long time the battle went this way, with advance and retreat in turn, and in both the Athenians had the worst.

Still, as long as their archers had arrows left and could use them, the Athenians held out, and the light-armed Aetolians retired before the arrows. But the captain of the archers was killed and his men were scattered. The soldiers, wearied by the constant repetition of the same exertions and hard pressed by the Aetolian javelins, at last turned and fled. They fell into pathless gullies and places they did not know, and so perished, for the Messenian Chromon, their guide, had also unfortunately been killed. A great many were overtaken in the pursuit by the swift-footed, light-armed Aetolians and fell beneath their javelins. The greater number, however, missed their road and rushed into a wood that had no way out, and the enemy soon set it on fire and burned it around them. Indeed the Athenian army fell victim to death in every form and suffered every vicissitude of flight. The survivors escaped with difficulty to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, from which they had set out. Many of the allies were killed, and about one hundred and twenty Athenian heavy infantry, not a man less, and all in the prime of life. These were by far the best men of the city of Athens to fall during this war. Among the slain was also Procles, the colleague of Demosthenes. The Athenians took up their dead from the Aetolians under truce, withdrew to Naupactus, and from there went in their ships to Athens. Demosthenes stayed behind in Naupactus and its neighborhood, afraid to face the Athenians after the disaster.
At about the same time the Athenians on the coast of Sicily sailed to Locris. They landed from their ships, defeated the Locrians who came out against them, and captured a fort on the river Halex.

The same summer the Aetolians had sent an embassy to Corinth and Lacedaemon before the Athenian expedition. It consisted of Tolophus, an Ophionian, Boriades, an Eurytanian, and Tisander, an Apodotian. They now obtained the dispatch of an army to help them against Naupactus, which had invited the Athenian invasion. Toward autumn the Lacedaemonians sent out three thousand heavy infantry of the allies, five hundred of them from Heraclea, the newly founded city in Trachis. Eurylochus, a Spartan, commanded them, with Macarius and Menedaius, also Spartans, at his side.

The army assembled at Delphi, and Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians. The road to Naupactus ran through their territory, and he also had in mind to detach them from Athens. In Locris his chief supporters were the Amphissians, who were alarmed by the hostility of the Phocians. They were the first to give hostages, and for fear of the invading army they induced the rest to do likewise. The first were their neighbors the Myonians, who held the most difficult of the passes. After them came the Ipnians, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians and Oeanthians, who all joined in the expedition. The Olpaeans gave hostages but did not accompany the invasion. The Hyaeans refused both, until Polis, one of their villages, was captured.

When his preparations were finished, Eurylochus lodged the hostages in Kytinium, in Doris, and advanced on Naupactus through Locrian country. Two Locrian towns, Oeneon and Eupalium, refused to join him, and he took them on the way. In the territory of Naupactus the Aetolians joined him. The army laid waste the land and took the suburb of the town, which had no walls, and then also Molycrium, a Corinthian colony subject to Athens. Meanwhile the Athenian Demosthenes had stayed near Naupactus since the affair in Aetolia. He heard of the army and feared for the town, so he went to the Acarnanians and persuaded them to relieve it, though not without difficulty, because he had left Leucas. They sent a thousand heavy infantry with him on his ships. These threw themselves into the place and saved it, for the length of its wall and the small number of its defenders would otherwise have put it in the gravest danger. Eurylochus and his companions found that this force had gone in and that storming the town was impossible. They withdrew, not to Peloponnese, but to the country once called Aeolis, now Calydon and Pleuron, to the places around it, and to Proschium in Aetolia. The Ambraciots had come and urged them to join in attacking Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia and Acarnania. They affirmed that conquering these countries would bring the whole continent into alliance with Lacedaemon. Eurylochus agreed and dismissed the Aetolians. With his army he stayed quietly in those parts until the Ambraciots should take the field and he could join them before Argos.

Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the Athenians in Sicily marched with their Hellenic allies against the Sicel town of Inessa, whose acropolis was held by the Syracusans. They were joined by those Sicels, subjects or allies of Syracuse, who had revolted from her and come over to their army. They attacked Inessa without being able to take it, and retired. During the retreat, the allies who were retreating behind the Athenians were attacked by the Syracusans from the fort, and a large part of their army was routed with great slaughter. After this, Laches and the Athenians from the ships made some descents on Locris. They defeated the Locrians, who came against them under Proxenus, son of Capaton, on the river Caicinus, took some arms and departed.

That same winter the Athenians purified Delos, it appears in obedience to a certain oracle. Pisistratus the tyrant had purified it before, though not the whole island, only the part visible from the temple. Now the whole island was purified, in this manner. They dug up all the graves of those who had died on Delos, and ordered that from then on nobody might die or give birth on the island. The dying and the women in labor were to be carried across to Rhenea. Rhenea lies so close to Delos that Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, dedicated it to the Delian Apollo by binding it to Delos with a chain, after he had added it to his other island conquests in the period of his naval ascendancy.

After the purification, the Athenians celebrated for the first time the Delian games, which are held every fifth year. In ancient times, indeed, there had been a great assembly of the Ionians and the neighboring islanders at Delos. They used to come to the festival, as the Ionians now do to that of Ephesus, and athletic and poetic contests took place there, and the cities brought choirs of dancers. Nothing is clearer on this point than the following verses of Homer, from a hymn to Apollo:

Phœbus, wherever you stray, far or near, Delos was still of all your haunts most dear. Thither the robed Ionians take their way With wife and child to keep your holiday, Invoke your favor on each manly game, And dance and sing in honor of your name.

That there was also a poetic contest, in which the Ionians went to compete, is again shown by the following verses from the same hymn. After celebrating the Delian dance of the women, he ends his song of praise with these verses, in which he also alludes to himself:

Well, may Apollo keep you all! and so, Sweethearts, good-bye — yet tell me not I go Out from your hearts; and if in after hours Some other wanderer in this world of ours Touch at your shores, and ask your maidens here Who sings the songs the sweetest to your ear, Think of me then, and answer with a smile, ‘A blind old man of Scio’s rocky isle.’

Homer thus attests that there was anciently a great assembly and festival at Delos. In later times the islanders and the Athenians continued to send choirs of dancers with sacrifices, but the contests and most of the ceremonies were abolished, probably through adversity. The Athenians now celebrated the games on this occasion, adding the novelty of horse-races.

That same winter the Ambraciots marched out against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand heavy infantry, as they had promised Eurylochus when they asked him to keep his army there. They invaded the Argive territory and occupied Olpae, a stronghold on a hill near the sea. The Acarnanians had once fortified it, and the nation used it as its court of assizes. It lies on the coast, about two miles and three-quarters from the city of Argos. The Acarnanians meanwhile sent part of their forces to relieve Argos. With the rest they encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and stop them from passing through to join the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to lead them, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off Peloponnese under Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, for their part, sent a messenger to their own city and begged them to come to their aid with their whole levy. They feared that the army of Eurylochus might fail to get through the Acarnanians, and that they would then have to fight alone, or could not retreat, even if they wanted to, without danger.

Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians, meanwhile, learned that the Ambraciots had reached Olpae. They set out in all haste from Proschium to join them. They crossed the Achelous and advanced through Acarnania, which they found empty, since its people had gone to the relief of Argos. On their right they had the city of the Stratians with its garrison, and on their left the rest of Acarnania. They passed through the territory of the Stratians, advanced through Phytia, and, skirting Medeon, through Limnaea. Then they left Acarnania behind and entered a friendly country, that of the Agraeans. From there they reached and crossed Mount Thymaus, which belongs to the Agraeans, and came down into the Argive territory after dark. They passed between the city of Argos and the Acarnanian posts at Crenae, and joined the Ambraciots at Olpae.

At daybreak the two forces united, sat down at the place called Metropolis and encamped. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships entered the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, bringing Demosthenes, two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few Amphilochians had already reached Argos. Most of the Amphilochians were held back by force by the Ambraciots. They were making ready to give battle to the enemy, and had chosen Demosthenes to command the whole allied army along with their own generals. Demosthenes led them near Olpae and encamped, a great ravine lying between the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive, and on the sixth both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked its opponents. Demosthenes feared that his right might be surrounded. In a sunken road overgrown with bushes he therefore hid some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops. At the moment of the onset they were to rise behind the enemy’s projecting left wing and attack it in the rear. When both sides were ready, they joined battle. Demosthenes stood on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians. The rest of the line consisted of the different divisions of the Acarnanians and the Amphilochian carters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up all mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though they did not reach the end of the wing. There Eurylochus and his men faced the Messenians and Demosthenes.

The Peloponnesians were well engaged, and their outflanking wing was about to turn the enemy’s right. Then the Acarnanians rose from the ambush, fell on them from behind, and broke them at the first attack, so that they did not even stand to resist. Panic spread, and most of their army fled, terrified beyond measure at the sight of the division of Eurylochus, their best troops, being cut to pieces. Demosthenes and his Messenians, who were posted in this part of the field, did most of the work. Meanwhile the Ambraciots (the best soldiers in those countries) and the troops on the right wing defeated the division facing them and pursued it as far as Argos. On their return from the pursuit they found their main body beaten. The Acarnanians pressed them hard, and they got back to Olpae with difficulty, suffering heavy loss on the way, since they rushed on without discipline or order. Only the Mantineans kept their ranks during the retreat, and better than any others in the army.

The battle lasted until evening. On the next day Menedaius took sole command, since Eurylochus and Macarius were dead. After so signal a defeat he was at a loss. He could not see how to stay and endure a siege, cut off by land and by the Athenian fleet at sea, and he could not see how to retreat safely either. So he opened a parley with Demosthenes and the Acarnanian generals, asking for a truce, permission to retreat, and the recovery of the dead. They gave him the dead, set up a trophy, and took up their own, about three hundred. They publicly refused the army the retreat he asked for. In secret, however, Demosthenes and his Acarnanian colleagues allowed the Mantineans, Menedaius and the other commanders and leading men of the Peloponnesians to leave without delay. Their aim was to strip the Ambraciots and the mercenary host of foreigners of their supporters, and above all to discredit the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians with the Hellenes in those parts, as traitors and self-seekers.

The enemy was taking up his dead and burying them in haste as best he could, and those who had obtained permission were secretly planning their retreat. Then word came to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city were on the march. They were coming with their whole levy through Amphilochia, in answer to the first message from Olpae, to join their countrymen there, and they knew nothing of what had happened. Demosthenes prepared to march against them with his army. Meanwhile he sent a strong division ahead at once to block the roads and seize the strong positions. In the meantime the Mantineans and the others covered by the agreement went out, pretending to gather herbs and firewood. They slipped away by twos and threes, picking up along the way the things they claimed to have come for. When they had gone some distance from Olpae, they quickened their pace. The Ambraciots and those of the rest who had gone out in larger parties saw them hurrying on. They pushed on in turn and began to run to catch them up. At first the Acarnanians thought that all of them alike were leaving without permission, and began to pursue the Peloponnesians. They believed they were being betrayed, and even threw a dart or two at some of their own generals, who tried to stop them and told them that leave had been granted. In the end, however, they let the Mantineans and Peloponnesians pass and killed only the Ambraciots, though it was hard, and a matter of much dispute, to tell whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. About two hundred were killed in this way. The rest escaped into the neighboring territory of Agraea and found refuge with Salynthius, the friendly king of the Agraeans.

Meanwhile the Ambraciots from the city reached Idomene. It consists of two lofty hills. The troops Demosthenes had sent ahead took the higher one after nightfall, without being seen by the Ambraciots, who had climbed the smaller and bivouacked below it. After supper, at nightfall, Demosthenes set out with the rest of the army. He himself took half his force toward the pass, and the remainder went by the Amphilochian hills. At dawn he fell on the Ambraciots while they were still in their beds. They knew nothing of what had happened and fully thought the newcomers were their own countrymen. Demosthenes had purposely put the Messenians in front, with orders to speak to them in the Doric dialect and so win the confidence of the sentinels, who could not see them, since it was still dark. So he routed their army the moment he attacked it. Most were killed where they lay, and the rest broke away in flight over the hills. The roads, however, were already occupied. The Amphilochians knew their own country, but the Ambraciots did not and could not tell which way to turn. Their armor was heavy, against a light-armed enemy. So they fell into ravines and into the ambushes laid for them, and perished there. In their many efforts to escape, some even turned to the sea, which was not far away. They saw the Athenian ships coasting along the shore just as the action was going on, and swam out to them. In their panic they thought it better to die, if die they must, at the hands of the Athenians than at those of the barbarous and detested Amphilochians. Of the large Ambraciot force destroyed in this way, only a few reached the city safely. The Acarnanians stripped the dead, set up a trophy, and returned to Argos.

Next day a herald came from the Ambraciots who had fled from Olpae to the Agraeans. He came to ask leave to take up the dead who had fallen after the first engagement, when they left the camp with the Mantineans and their companions, without having, as these had, permission to do so. He saw the arms of the Ambraciots from the city and was astonished at their number. He knew nothing of the disaster and fancied they were the arms of his own party. Someone asked him what astonished him so much and how many of them had been killed. This man in his turn fancied that he was the herald from the troops at Idomene. The herald answered: “About two hundred.” His questioner caught him up, saying: “Why, the arms you see here are those of more than a thousand.” The herald replied: “Then they are not the arms of those who fought with us?” The other answered: “Yes, they are, if at least you fought at Idomene yesterday.” “But we fought no one yesterday; it was the day before, in the retreat.” “However that may be, we fought yesterday against those who came to reinforce you from the city of the Ambraciots.” When the herald heard this and understood that the reinforcement from the city had been destroyed, he broke out in wailing. Stunned by the magnitude of the present evils, he left at once, without performing his errand and without asking again for the dead bodies. This was indeed by far the greatest disaster that befell any one Hellenic city in so few days during this war. I have not set down the number of the dead, because the figure given seems so out of proportion to the size of the city that it is incredible. In any case I know this: if the Acarnanians and Amphilochians had wished to take Ambracia, as the Athenians and Demosthenes advised, they would have taken it without a blow. As it was, they feared that if the Athenians held it, they would be worse neighbors than the present ones.

After this the Acarnanians gave a third of the spoils to the Athenians and divided the rest among their own towns. The Athenians’ share was captured on the voyage home. The arms now deposited in the Attic temples are three hundred panoplies, which the Acarnanians set aside for Demosthenes and which he brought to Athens himself. This exploit made his return home after the Aetolian disaster less dangerous. The Athenians in the twenty ships also went off to Naupactus. When Demosthenes and the Athenians had gone, the Acarnanians and Amphilochians allowed the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who had taken refuge with Salynthius and the Agraeans to leave freely from Oeniadae, to which they had moved from the country of Salynthius. They also concluded with the Ambraciots a treaty and alliance for one hundred years, on the following terms. It was to be a defensive, not an offensive alliance. The Ambraciots could not be required to march with the Acarnanians against the Peloponnesians, nor the Acarnanians with the Ambraciots against the Athenians. Besides this, the Ambraciots were to give up the places and hostages they held from the Amphilochians, and not to help Anactorium, which was at enmity with the Acarnanians. With this settlement they ended the war. After this the Corinthians sent a garrison of their own citizens to Ambracia: three hundred heavy infantry under Xenocleides, son of Euthycles, who reached their destination after a difficult journey over land. Such was the story of the affair of Ambracia.

That same winter the Athenians in Sicily landed from their ships on the territory of Himera, in concert with the Sicels, who had invaded its borders from the interior, and then sailed to the islands of Aeolus. When they returned to Rhegium, they found that the Athenian general Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, had arrived to take Laches’ place in command of the fleet. The allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and persuaded the Athenians to send more ships to help them. They pointed out that the Syracusans, who already controlled the land, were working to assemble a navy, so that a few ships should no longer keep them from the sea. The Athenians set about manning forty ships to send to Sicily. They thought the war there would end sooner, and they also wanted to give their navy exercise. One of the generals, Pythodorus, was accordingly sent out with a few ships. Sophocles, son of Sostratides, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles, were to follow with the main body. Meanwhile Pythodorus had taken over Laches’ ships. Toward the end of winter he sailed against the Locrian fort that Laches had taken before, and came back after being beaten in battle by the Locrians.

In the first days of this spring a stream of fire poured out of Etna, as on earlier occasions, and destroyed some land of the Catanians, who live on Mount Etna, the largest mountain in Sicily. Fifty years, it is said, had passed since the last eruption, and there had been three in all since the Hellenes settled Sicily. Such were the events of this winter, and with it ended the sixth year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 12 — Seventh Year of the War—Occupation of Pylos—Surrender of the Spartan Army in Sphacteria
paragraphs: The next summer, about the time the corn was coming into ear, ten Syracusan ships and as many Locrian vessels sailed to Messina in Sicily. The inhabitants had invited them, and they occupied the town; Messina revolted from the Athenians. The Syracusans brought this about chiefly because they saw that the place gave access to Sicily, and feared that the Athenians might later use it as a base for attacking them with a larger force. The Locrians acted because they wished to make war from both sides of the strait and to reduce their enemies, the people of Rhegium. Meanwhile the Locrians had invaded Rhegian territory with all their forces, to stop the Rhegians from helping Messina, and also at the urging of some exiles from Rhegium who were with them. The long factions that had torn that town left it for the moment unable to resist, and this was a further temptation to the invaders. After devastating the country, the Locrian land forces withdrew; their ships stayed to guard Messina, while others were being manned to go to the same place and carry on the war from there.

About the same time, in the spring, before the corn was ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and settled down to lay waste the country. Meanwhile the Athenians sent off to Sicily the forty ships they had been preparing, with the remaining generals Eurymedon and Sophocles; their colleague Pythodorus had already gone ahead. These generals were also instructed, as they sailed by, to look after the Corcyraeans in the town, who were being plundered by the exiles in the mountain. Sixty Peloponnesian vessels had lately sailed to support these exiles, in the belief that the famine raging in the city would make it easy to reduce. Demosthenes also had remained without employment since his return from Acarnania. He now applied for permission, and obtained it, to use the fleet if he wished on the coast of Peloponnese.

Off Laconia they heard that the Peloponnesian ships were already at Corcyra. Eurymedon and Sophocles then wished to hurry to the island, but Demosthenes required them first to touch at Pylos and do what was needed there before continuing their voyage. While they were still objecting, a squall came on and carried the fleet into Pylos. Demosthenes at once urged them to fortify the place, saying that this was why he had come on the voyage. He pointed out that there was plenty of stone and timber on the spot, that the place was strong by nature, and that it and much of the country round it were unoccupied. Pylos, or Coryphasium as the Lacedaemonians call it, is about forty-five miles from Sparta, in the old country of the Messenians. The commanders told him there was no lack of desert headlands in Peloponnese, if he wished to put the city to expense by occupying them. He thought, however, that this place was different from others of the kind because it had a harbor close by. The Messenians, the old natives of the country, spoke the same dialect as the Lacedaemonians, and could do them the greatest mischief by raids from it, while also serving as a trusty garrison.

He spoke to the captains of companies about it, but failed to persuade either the generals or the soldiers, and he remained inactive with the rest because of bad weather. Then the soldiers themselves, having nothing to do, were seized with a sudden impulse to go round and fortify the place. They set to work in earnest. They had no iron tools, so they picked up stones and fitted them together as they happened to match. Where mortar was needed, they carried it on their backs for lack of hods, stooping so that it would stay on and clasping their hands behind them to keep it from falling off. They spared no effort to finish the most vulnerable points before the Lacedaemonians arrived; most of the place was strong enough by nature without further fortification.

The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, were celebrating a festival. At first they also made light of the news, thinking that whenever they chose to take the field the enemy would evacuate the place at once or be easily driven out by force; the absence of their army before Athens also had something to do with their delay. The Athenians fortified the place on the land side, and wherever it most needed it, in six days. They left Demosthenes with five ships to garrison it, and the main body of the fleet hurried on its voyage to Corcyra and Sicily.

The Peloponnesians in Attica heard of the occupation of Pylos and at once hurried home. The Lacedaemonians and their king Agis thought the matter concerned them closely. Besides, the invasion had begun early in the season, while the corn was still green, and most of their troops were short of provisions. The weather too was unusually bad for the time of year, and greatly distressed the army. Many reasons thus combined to hasten their departure and to make this a very short invasion: they stayed only fifteen days in Attica.

About the same time the Athenian general Simonides gathered a few Athenians from the garrisons and a number of the allies in those parts, and took Eion in Thrace by treachery. Eion was a Mendaean colony and hostile to Athens. But no sooner had he taken it than the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans came up and drove him out, with the loss of many of his soldiers.

When the Peloponnesians returned from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the Perioeci set out at once for Pylos; the other Lacedaemonians followed more slowly, since they had just come in from another campaign. Word was also sent around Peloponnese to come up to Pylos as quickly as possible. The sixty Peloponnesian ships were sent for from Corcyra; their crews dragged them across the isthmus of Leucas, they passed unperceived by the Athenian squadron at Zacynthus, and they reached Pylos, where the land forces had arrived before them. Before the Peloponnesian fleet sailed in, Demosthenes found time to send out two ships unobserved, to tell Eurymedon and the Athenians on board the fleet at Zacynthus of the danger at Pylos and to summon them to his assistance. While the ships hurried on their voyage in obedience to his orders, the Lacedaemonians prepared to assault the fort by land and sea. They hoped to capture with ease a work built in haste and held by a feeble garrison. Meanwhile they expected the Athenian ships to arrive from Zacynthus, and intended, if they failed to take the place before then, to block the entrances of the harbor so that the Athenians could not anchor inside it. For the island of Sphacteria stretches in a line close in front of the harbor, making it safe and narrowing its entrances. It leaves a passage for two ships on the side nearest Pylos and the Athenian fortifications, and for eight or nine on the side toward the rest of the mainland. The island was entirely covered with wood, and since it was uninhabited it had no paths; it was about one mile and five furlongs in length. The Lacedaemonians meant to close the inlets with a line of ships placed close together, with their prows turned toward the sea. Meanwhile, fearing that the enemy might use the island to operate against them, they carried some heavy infantry over to it and stationed others along the coast. In this way the island and the continent would alike be hostile to the Athenians, who would be unable to land on either. The shore of Pylos itself, outside the inlet toward the open sea, has no harbor, and so offered no point the Athenians could use as a base to relieve their countrymen. The Lacedaemonians therefore would in all probability become masters of the place without a sea-fight or any risk, since it had been occupied on the spur of the moment and was unfurnished with provisions. This being determined, they carried over to the island the heavy infantry, drafted by lot from all the companies. Some others had crossed over before in relief parties, but those who were left there at the last numbered four hundred and twenty, with their Helot attendants, and were commanded by Epitadas, son of Molobrus.

Meanwhile Demosthenes, seeing that the Lacedaemonians were about to attack him by sea and land at once, was not idle himself. He drew up the galleys that remained to him, out of those that had been left him, under the fortification and enclosed them in a stockade. He armed the sailors taken from them with poor shields, most of them made of osier, since it was impossible to procure arms in such a desert place. Even these had been obtained from a thirty-oared Messenian privateer and a boat belonging to some Messenians who happened to have come to them. Among these Messenians were forty heavy infantry, whom he used along with the rest. He posted most of his men, unarmed and armed, at the best fortified and strongest points of the place toward the interior, with orders to repel any attack by the land forces. From his whole force he picked sixty heavy infantry and a few archers, and with these he went outside the wall down to the sea, where he thought the enemy would most likely attempt to land. The ground there was difficult and rocky, and faced the open sea. But this was the weakest part of the wall, and he thought that this fact would encourage the enemy’s ardor: the Athenians, confident in their naval superiority, had paid little attention to their defenses here, and the enemy, if he could force a landing, might feel sure of taking the place. Going down to the water’s edge at this point, he posted his heavy infantry to prevent a landing if possible, and encouraged them in the following terms:

“Soldiers and comrades in this adventure, I hope that in our present strait none of you will try to show his cleverness by reckoning up exactly all the perils around us. I hope you will instead hurry to close with the enemy, without stopping to count the odds, and see in this your best chance of safety. In emergencies like ours, calculation is out of place; the sooner we face the danger, the better. In my judgment, too, most of the chances are on our side, if only we stand fast and do not throw away our advantages out of awe at the enemy’s numbers. One point in our favor is the awkwardness of the landing. But this helps us only if we hold our ground. If we give way, the landing will be easy enough, in spite of its natural difficulty, because nobody will be there to stop it. And the enemy will at once become more formidable, since retreat will be harder for him — if we succeed in repulsing him, that is, which we shall find easier to do while he is still on board his ships than after he has landed and meets us on equal terms. As for his numbers, they need not alarm you too much. However large they are, he can engage only in small detachments, because many ships cannot bring to at once. Besides, we are not facing the numerical superiority of an army on land with everything else equal, but that of troops on board ship, on an element where many lucky chances are needed for them to act effectively. I therefore consider that his difficulties may fairly be weighed against our shortage of men. And I charge you, as Athenians who know from experience what it means to land from ships on hostile territory, and how impossible it is to drive back an enemy who is resolute enough to stand his ground and who is not frightened away by the surf and the terror of ships sailing in, to stand fast now, beat the enemy back at the water’s edge, and save yourselves and the place.”

Encouraged by these words of Demosthenes, the Athenians felt more confident, went down to meet the enemy, and took up positions along the edge of the sea. The Lacedaemonians now advanced and assaulted the fortification with their land forces and, at the same moment, with their ships, forty-three in number, under the admiral Thrasymelidas, son of Cratesicles, a Spartan. His attack came just where Demosthenes had expected it. The Athenians thus had to defend themselves on two sides, from the land and from the sea. The enemy rowed up in small detachments, each relieving the one before — many could not bring to at once — and showed great ardor, cheering each other on in the effort to force a passage and take the fortification. The man who distinguished himself most was Brasidas. He was captain of a galley, and he saw that the captains and steersmen, daunted by the difficulty of the position, were hanging back even where a landing seemed possible, for fear of wrecking their vessels. He shouted to them that they must not let the enemy fortify himself in their country just to save timber, but must shatter their vessels and force a landing. And he told the allies that in such a moment they must not hesitate: in return for the many benefits they had received from Lacedaemon, they must sacrifice their ships, run them boldly aground, get ashore one way or another, and make themselves masters of the place and its garrison.

Not content with this exhortation, he forced his own steersman to run the ship ashore. He stepped onto the gangway and was trying to land when the Athenians cut him down; after many wounds he fainted. He fell into the bows, and his shield slipped from his arm into the sea. It was washed ashore and picked up by the Athenians, who later used it for the trophy they set up for this attack. The rest also did their best, but could not land, because the ground was difficult and the Athenians held on without flinching. It was a strange reversal of the usual order of things. Athenians were fighting from the land, and Laconian land at that, against Lacedaemonians coming from the sea; and Lacedaemonians were trying to land from shipboard in their own country, now hostile, to attack Athenians. Yet at that time the Lacedaemonians were famous chiefly as an inland people, superior by land, and the Athenians as a maritime people with a navy that had no equal.

The Peloponnesians continued their attacks during that day and most of the next, and then desisted. The day after, they sent some of their ships to Asine for timber to make engines. With these they hoped to take, in spite of its height, the wall opposite the harbor, where the landing was easiest. At this moment the Athenian fleet from Zacynthus arrived, now numbering fifty ships, reinforced by some of the ships on guard at Naupactus and by four Chian vessels. They saw the coast and the island both crowded with heavy infantry, and the hostile ships in the harbor showing no sign of sailing out. At a loss where to anchor, they sailed for the moment to the desert island of Prote, not far off, where they passed the night. The next day they got under way, ready to engage in the open sea if the enemy chose to put out to meet them, and determined, if he did not, to sail in and attack him. The Lacedaemonians did not put out to sea. They had failed to close the inlets as they had intended, and they stayed quiet on shore, manning their ships and getting ready to fight in the harbor, which is a fairly large one, if anyone sailed in.

Seeing this, the Athenians advanced against them by each inlet. They fell on the enemy’s fleet, most of which was by this time afloat and in line, and put it to flight at once. They chased it as far as the short distance allowed, disabled a good many vessels and took five, one with its crew on board. They dashed in at the rest that had taken refuge on shore, and battered some that were still being manned before they could put out; they also lashed other, empty ships whose crews had fled to their own ships and towed them off. At this sight the Lacedaemonians, maddened by a disaster that cut off their men on the island, rushed to the rescue. They went into the sea with their heavy armor, laid hold of the ships and tried to drag them back, each man thinking that success depended on his own exertions. The melee was great, and quite contrary to the naval tactics usual to the two combatants. The Lacedaemonians, in their excitement and dismay, were actually fighting a sea-fight on land, while the victorious Athenians, in their eagerness to push their success as far as possible, were fighting a land-fight from their ships. After great exertions and numerous wounds on both sides, they separated. The Lacedaemonians saved their empty ships, except those first taken. Both parties returned to their camps, and the Athenians set up a trophy, gave back the dead, secured the wrecks, and at once began to cruise round the island and keep jealous watch on it, with its intercepted garrison. The Peloponnesians on the mainland, whose contingents had now all come up, stayed where they were before Pylos.

News of what had happened at Pylos reached Sparta. The disaster was thought so serious that the Lacedaemonians resolved to send the authorities down to the camp, to decide on the spot what was best to do. There they saw that they could not help their men, and they did not want to risk seeing them starved into submission or overpowered by numbers. So they determined, with the consent of the Athenian generals, to conclude an armistice at Pylos, send envoys to Athens to obtain a convention, and try to get their men back as quickly as possible.
The generals accepted their offers, and an armistice was concluded on the following terms:

That the Lacedaemonians should bring to Pylos, and deliver up to the Athenians, the ships that had fought in the late engagement and all the vessels of war in Laconia, and should make no attack on the fortification by land or by sea.

That the Athenians should allow the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to send over to the men on the island a fixed ration of ready-kneaded corn: two quarts of barley meal, one pint of wine and a piece of meat for each man, and half as much for a servant.
That the Lacedaemonians should send this allowance over in full view of the Athenians, and that no boat should sail to the island except openly.
That the Athenians should go on guarding the island as before, but without landing on it, and should not attack the Peloponnesian troops by land or by sea.
That if either party broke any of these terms in even the slightest particular, the armistice should be void at once.

That the armistice should remain in force until the Lacedaemonian envoys came back from Athens, the Athenians sending them there in a galley and bringing them back; that it should end on their arrival; and that the Athenians should then return the ships in the same condition in which they had received them.
Such were the terms of the armistice. The ships, sixty in number, were delivered over, and the envoys were sent off accordingly. When they arrived at Athens they spoke as follows:

“Athenians, the Lacedaemonians sent us to try to find a way of settling the matter of our men on the island, a way that will serve our interests and also protect our dignity in misfortune as far as circumstances allow. We can venture to speak at some length without breaking with the habit of our country. We are men of few words where many are not needed, but we can say more when there is an important matter to explain and some purpose to be served by explaining it. Meanwhile we ask you not to take what we say in a hostile spirit, nor as if we thought you ignorant and wished to lecture you. Take it rather as a suggestion about the best course to follow, put to intelligent judges. You can now, if you choose, turn your present success to advantage: you can keep what you have won and gain honor and reputation besides. You can avoid the mistake of those who meet with extraordinary good fortune and are led on by hope to keep reaching for more, because they have already succeeded beyond their expectation. Those who have known the most changes of good and bad fortune are also, rightly, the least trustful of their prosperity; and to teach your city and ours this lesson, experience has not been lacking.

“To be convinced of this, you have only to look at our present misfortune. What power in Hellas stood higher than we did? And yet we have come to you, although we once thought ourselves better able to grant what we are now here to ask. Nevertheless, our power has not decayed to bring us to this, nor did aggrandizement turn our heads. No, our resources are what they have always been, and what failed us was our judgment, a failing to which all are equally liable. So the prosperity your city now enjoys, and the strength it has lately gained, must not lead you to imagine that fortune will always be with you. Sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they keep a clear head in adversity. They hold that war, far from staying within the limit a combatant may wish to set for it, will run the course its chances dictate. Not being puffed up by confidence in military success, they are therefore less likely to come to grief, and readiest to make peace, if they can, while their fortune lasts. This, Athenians, you have a good opportunity to do now with us. You can thus escape the disasters that may follow if you refuse, and the charge that even your present advantages were owed to accident, when you might have left behind a reputation for power and wisdom that nothing could endanger.

“The Lacedaemonians therefore invite you to make a treaty and end the war. They offer peace and alliance, and the most friendly and intimate relations between us in every way and on every occasion; and in return they ask for the men on the island. They think it better for both sides not to hold out to the end, in case some lucky accident lets the men break out, or the pressure of blockade forces them to give in. Indeed, if great enmities are ever to be truly settled, we think the settlement will come not through revenge and military success, and by forcing an opponent to swear to a treaty that works against him. It will come when the luckier combatant gives up these privileges, lets gentler feelings guide him, beats his rival in generosity, and grants peace on more moderate terms than the other expected. From that moment, instead of the debt of revenge that violence must bring, his adversary owes a debt of generosity to be repaid in kind, and honor inclines him to keep his agreement. Men also act in this way more often toward their greatest enemies than in quarrels of less importance. And they are by nature as glad to yield to those who first yield to them as they are prone to be provoked by arrogance into risks that their own judgment condemns.

“To apply this to ourselves: if peace was ever desirable for both sides, it surely is so now, before anything irremediable happens to us and makes us hate you forever, personally as well as politically, and makes you lose the advantages we now offer you. The outcome is still in doubt. You have reputation and our friendship in prospect, and we have the chance to compromise on our misfortune before anything fatal occurs. Let us be reconciled, and choose peace instead of war for ourselves, and give the rest of the Hellenes relief from their sufferings, for which, be sure, they will think they have chiefly you to thank. They do not know which side began the war they labor under, but the peace that ends it, since it depends on your decision, will be laid to your door by their gratitude. By such a decision you can become firm friends with the Lacedaemonians, at their own invitation, which you do not extort from them but oblige them by accepting.
