And consider the advantages likely to follow from this friendship: when Attica and Sparta are at one, the rest of Hellas, be sure, will remain in respectful inferiority before its heads.”

Such were the words of the Lacedaemonians. They thought that the Athenians, already wanting a truce and held back only by Lacedaemonian opposition, would gladly accept a peace freely offered, and give back the men. The Athenians, however, held the men on the island, and thought the treaty would be ready for them whenever they chose to make it; so they reached for something more. The first to encourage them in this policy was Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, a popular leader of the time with great power over the multitude. He persuaded them to reply as follows. First, the men on the island must surrender themselves and their arms, and be brought to Athens. Next, the Lacedaemonians must restore Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen and Achaia. These places had been won not by arms but by the previous convention, under which Athens herself had ceded them in a moment of disaster, when she needed a truce more than she did now. When this was done, the Lacedaemonians might take back their men, and make a truce for as long as both sides agreed.

The envoys made no reply to this answer. They asked instead that commissioners be chosen to confer with them on each point, so that they could talk the matter over quietly and try to reach some agreement. Cleon then attacked them violently. He said he had known from the start that their intentions were not honest, and that it was clear enough now, since they refused to speak before the people and wanted to confer in secret with a committee of two or three. No, he said, if they meant anything honest, let them say it out before everyone. The Lacedaemonians saw that, whatever concessions they might be ready to make in their misfortune, they could not speak before the multitude and lose credit with their allies over a negotiation that might still come to nothing. They saw, too, that the Athenians would never grant their request on moderate terms. So they returned from Athens having accomplished nothing.

Their arrival at once put an end to the armistice at Pylos, and the Lacedaemonians asked for their ships back, according to the convention. The Athenians, however, alleged an attack on the fort in violation of the truce, and other grievances that hardly seemed worth mentioning, and refused to give the ships back, insisting on the clause by which the slightest infringement made the armistice void. The Lacedaemonians denied the violation and protested against the Athenians’ bad faith over the ships. Then they went away and addressed themselves earnestly to the war. Hostilities at Pylos were now carried on vigorously by both sides. The Athenians cruised round the island all day with two ships going in different directions. By night, except on the seaward side in windy weather, they anchored round it with their whole fleet, which had been reinforced by twenty ships from Athens, come to aid in the blockade, and now numbered seventy ships. The Peloponnesians, meanwhile, remained encamped on the continent, making attacks on the fort and watching for any opportunity that might offer itself to deliver their men.

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies in Sicily had finished preparing the reinforcement we left them assembling, and had added it to the squadron guarding Messina. From there they carried on the war. The Locrians urged them on most, out of hatred for the Rhegians, whose territory they had invaded with all their forces. The Syracusans also wanted to try their fortune at sea. They saw that the Athenians had only a few ships actually at Rhegium, and they heard that the main fleet meant to join them was occupied in blockading the island. A naval victory, they thought, would let them blockade Rhegium by sea and land and reduce it easily. That success would at once put their affairs on a solid footing, since the promontory of Rhegium in Italy and Messina in Sicily lie so close together that the Athenians could not cruise against them and command the strait. The strait in question is the sea between Rhegium and Messina, at the point where Sicily comes nearest to the continent. It is the Charybdis through which the story has Ulysses sail. The narrowness of the passage, and the strength of the current pouring in from the vast Tyrrhenian and Sicilian seas, have rightly given it a bad reputation.

In this strait the Syracusans and their allies were forced to fight late in the day over the passage of a boat. They put out with rather more than thirty ships against sixteen Athenian and eight Rhegian vessels. The Athenians defeated them, and they hurried off, each for himself, to their own stations at Messina and Rhegium, having lost one ship; night came on before the battle was finished. After this the Locrians withdrew from the Rhegian territory, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies joined together and anchored at Cape Pelorus, in the territory of Messina, where their land forces joined them. The Athenians and Rhegians sailed up and, seeing the ships unmanned, attacked. In this attack they in their turn lost one vessel, which was caught by a grappling iron, though the crew saved themselves by swimming. After this the Syracusans went on board their ships, and while they were being towed along the shore to Messina, the Athenians attacked them again. But the Syracusans suddenly put out to sea, became the attackers, and made the Athenians lose another vessel. They had held their own in the voyage along the shore and in the fighting just described, and they now sailed on into the harbor of Messina.

Meanwhile the Athenians had been warned that Camarina was about to be betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his party, and sailed there. The Messinese took the opportunity to attack their Chalcidian neighbor, Naxos, with all their forces by sea and land. On the first day they forced the Naxians to keep inside their walls and laid waste their country. On the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land on the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers to help against the Messinese. The Naxians were elated at the sight, and believed that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them. They suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked and routed the Messinese, and killed more than a thousand of them. The rest suffered severely in their retreat home, for the barbarians attacked them on the road and cut off most of them. The ships put in to Messina and afterwards dispersed to their different homes. The Leontines and their allies, together with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against Messina, now weakened. The Athenians attacked with their ships on the side of the harbor, and the land forces on the side of the town. But the Messinese sallied out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster. They suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. When the Athenians saw this, they landed from their ships, fell on the Messinese in their disorder, and chased them back into the town. Then they set up a trophy and withdrew to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos were still besieging the Lacedaemonians on the island, while the Peloponnesian forces on the continent stayed where they were. The blockade was very laborious for the Athenians because of the want of food and water. There was no spring except one in the citadel of Pylos itself, and that was not large, so most of them had to dig up the shingle on the beach and drink whatever water they could find. They also suffered from want of room, since they were encamped in a narrow space. As there was no anchorage for the ships, some of the men took their meals on shore in turn while the others lay at anchor out at sea. But what discouraged them most was the unexpectedly long time it took to reduce a body of men shut up on a desert island with only brackish water to drink. They had imagined it would take only a few days. The reason was that the Lacedaemonians had advertised for volunteers to carry ground corn, wine, cheese and any other food useful in a siege into the island. They offered high prices, and promised freedom to any of the Helots who succeeded. The Helots were therefore most eager to engage in this risky traffic. They set out from various parts of Peloponnese and ran in by night on the seaward side of the island. They were best pleased when they could catch a wind to carry them in. It was easier to elude the lookout of the galleys when the wind blew from the sea, because the galleys could not then anchor round the island. The Helots, for their part, had their boats valued at their price in money, and ran them ashore without caring how they landed, since they were sure to find the soldiers waiting for them at the landing places. But all who risked it in fair weather were taken. Divers also swam in under water from the harbor, dragging along by a cord, in skins, poppyseed mixed with honey and crushed linseed. At first these went unnoticed, but afterwards a lookout was kept for them. In short, both sides tried every possible contrivance, the one to throw in provisions and the other to prevent them from coming in.

At Athens, meanwhile, the news that the army was in great distress, and that corn was finding its way in to the men on the island, caused no small perplexity. The Athenians began to fear that winter would come and find them still engaged in the blockade. They saw that it would then be impossible to convoy provisions round Peloponnese. The country offered no resources in itself, and even in summer they could not send round enough. A place without harbors could no longer be blockaded, and the men would either escape because the siege was abandoned, or would watch for bad weather and sail out in the boats that brought in their corn. What alarmed them still more was the attitude of the Lacedaemonians. The Athenians thought they must feel themselves on strong ground not to send any more envoys, and they began to repent of having rejected the treaty. Cleon saw that he was regarded with disfavor for having stood in the way of the convention. He now said that their informants did not speak the truth. When the messengers recommended that, if the Athenians did not believe them, they should send commissioners to see for themselves, the Athenians chose Cleon himself and Theagenes as commissioners. Cleon realized that he would now be obliged either to say what the men he was slandering had already said, or to be proved a liar if he said the contrary. He saw that the Athenians were not altogether unwilling to make a fresh expedition, and told them that, instead of sending commissioners and wasting their time and opportunities, they ought to sail against the men if they believed what they were told. Then he pointed at Nicias, son of Niceratus, who was then general and whom he hated, and said tauntingly that it would be easy, if they had real men for generals, to sail with a force and take the men on the island. If he himself were in command, he said, he would have done it.

Nicias saw the Athenians murmuring against Cleon for not sailing now, if it seemed so easy to him. He saw too that he himself was the object of the attack, and he told Cleon that, as far as the generals were concerned, he might take whatever force he chose and make the attempt. At first Cleon took this resignation for a mere figure of speech and was ready to go. But when he found that it was meant seriously, he drew back. He said that Nicias, not he, was general, for he was now frightened, having never supposed that Nicias would go so far as to step down in his favor. Nicias, however, repeated his offer, resigned the command against Pylos, and called the Athenians to witness that he did so. And as a crowd is apt to do, the more Cleon shrank from the expedition and tried to back out of what he had said, the more they urged Nicias to hand over his command and clamored at Cleon to go. At last, not knowing how to get out of his words, Cleon undertook the expedition. He came forward and said that he was not afraid of the Lacedaemonians, and that he would sail without taking anyone from the city with him, except the Lemnians and Imbrians who were at Athens, some targeteers who had come up from Aenus, and four hundred archers from other quarters. With these and the soldiers at Pylos, he said, he would within twenty days either bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them on the spot. The Athenians could not help laughing at his folly. Sensible men, however, comforted themselves with the thought that they must gain either way: either they would be rid of Cleon, which they rather hoped, or, if disappointed in that, they would reduce the Lacedaemonians.

When he had settled everything in the assembly and the Athenians had voted him the command of the expedition, he chose Demosthenes, one of the generals at Pylos, as his colleague, and pushed forward the preparations for the voyage. He chose Demosthenes because he heard that he was contemplating a descent on the island. The soldiers, distressed by the difficulties of their position and rather besieged than besiegers, were eager to fight it out, and the burning of the island had increased the general’s confidence. He had at first been afraid. The island had never been inhabited and was almost entirely covered with wood, without paths, and he thought this favored the enemy: he might land with a large force and still suffer loss from an attack out of an unseen position. The wood would in great measure hide the enemy’s mistakes and forces from him, while every blunder of his own troops would at once be detected, and the enemy could fall on him unexpectedly wherever they pleased, since the attack would always be in their power. If, on the other hand, he forced them to fight in the thicket, the smaller number who knew the country would, he thought, have the advantage over the larger number who did not. And his own army might be cut off unnoticed, in spite of its numbers, as the men would not be able to see where to help each other.

The Aetolian disaster, which had been mainly caused by the wood, had not a little to do with these reflections. Meanwhile one of the soldiers, who were compelled by want of room to land on the extremities of the island and take their dinners, with outposts posted to prevent a surprise, set fire to a little of the wood without meaning to. As it came on to blow soon afterwards, almost the whole wood was consumed before they were aware of it. Demosthenes was now able for the first time to see how numerous the Lacedaemonians really were, for up to this moment he had been under the impression that they took in provisions for a smaller number. He also saw that the Athenians thought success important and were anxious about it, and that it was now easier to land on the island. He accordingly got ready for the attempt, sent for troops from the allies in the neighborhood, and pushed forward his other preparations. At this moment Cleon arrived at Pylos with the troops he had asked for, having sent word ahead that he was coming. The first step the two generals took after meeting was to send a herald to the camp on the mainland. He was to ask whether the Lacedaemonians there were disposed to avoid all risk and to order the men on the island to surrender themselves and their arms, to be kept in gentle custody until some general convention should be concluded.

When this proposal was rejected, the generals let one day pass. The next day they embarked all their heavy infantry on a few ships and put out by night. A little before dawn they landed, about eight hundred strong, on both sides of the island, from the open sea and from the harbor, and advanced at a run against the first post on the island.

The enemy had distributed his force as follows. In this first post there were about thirty heavy infantry. The center and most level part of the island, where the water was, was held by the main body under Epitadas, their commander. A small party guarded the very end of the island toward Pylos, which was precipitous on the seaward side and very difficult to attack from the land. There was also a sort of old fort there, of stones roughly put together, which they thought might be useful to them if they were forced to retreat. Such was their disposition.

The advanced post thus attacked by the Athenians was put to the sword at once. The men were scarcely out of bed and still arming, for the landing had taken them by surprise: they had fancied that the ships were only sailing as usual to their stations for the night. As soon as day broke, the rest of the army landed. This was all the crews of rather more than seventy ships, except the lowest rank of oarsmen, with the arms they carried, eight hundred archers and as many targeteers, the Messenian reinforcements, and all the other troops on duty round Pylos, except the garrison on the fort. Demosthenes had divided them, as his tactics required, into companies of two hundred, more or less, and had them occupy the highest points. His aim was to paralyze the enemy by surrounding him on every side, leaving him without any tangible adversary and exposed to the cross-fire of their host. If he attacked in front, he would be plied by those in his rear, and if he moved against those on one flank, by those on the other. In short, wherever he went he would have assailants behind him, and these were light-armed assailants, the most awkward of all. Arrows, darts, stones and slings made them formidable at a distance, and there was no means of getting at them at close quarters, for they could conquer in flight, and the moment their pursuer turned they were upon him. Such was the idea that inspired Demosthenes in conceiving the descent, and that governed its execution.

Meanwhile the main body of the troops on the island, that under Epitadas, saw their outpost cut off and an army advancing against them. They closed their ranks and pressed forward to engage the Athenian heavy infantry in front of them, with the light troops on their flanks and rear. But they could not engage, or make use of their superior skill. The light troops kept them in check on either side with their missiles, and the heavy infantry stayed where they were instead of advancing to meet them. Wherever the light troops ran up and came too close, the Lacedaemonians routed them, yet the light troops retreated fighting. They were lightly equipped and easily got a start in their flight, because of the difficult and rugged ground, on an island hitherto desert, over which the Lacedaemonians could not pursue them in their heavy armor.

After this skirmishing had lasted some little while, the Lacedaemonians became unable to dash out with the same speed as before upon the points attacked. The light troops, finding that they now fought with less vigor, grew more confident. They could see with their own eyes that they were many times more numerous than the enemy. They were now more familiar with his appearance and found him less terrible, since the result had not justified the fears they had felt when they first landed, in slavish dismay at the idea of attacking Lacedaemonians. Their fear therefore changed to disdain, and they rushed all together upon the Lacedaemonians with loud shouts, and pelted them with stones, darts and arrows, whichever came first to hand. The shouting that accompanied their onset confounded the Lacedaemonians, who were unaccustomed to this mode of fighting. Dust rose from the newly burnt wood, and it was impossible to see ahead, with arrows and stones flying through clouds of dust from the hands of numerous assailants. The Lacedaemonians now had to sustain a rough conflict. Their caps would not keep out the arrows, darts had broken off in the armor of the wounded, and they themselves were helpless to strike back, because they could not use their eyes to see what was before them and could not hear the words of command for the uproar the enemy raised. Danger surrounded them on every side, and they had no hope of any means of defense or safety.

At last, after many had been wounded in the confined space in which they were fighting, they formed in close order and retired on the fort at the end of the island, which was not far off, where their friends held the post. The moment they gave way, the light troops became bolder and pressed upon them, shouting louder than ever. They killed as many as they came up with in the retreat, but most of the Lacedaemonians made good their escape to the fort. With the garrison there they ranged themselves along its whole extent, to repulse the enemy wherever it could be assailed. The Athenians pursued but, because of the strength of the ground, could not surround and hem them in. They attacked in front and tried to storm the position. For a long time, indeed for most of the day, both sides held out against all the torments of the battle, thirst and sun, the one trying to drive the enemy from the high ground, the other to maintain himself on it. It was now easier for the Lacedaemonians to defend themselves than before, as they could not be surrounded on the flanks.

The struggle began to seem endless, when the commander of the Messenians came to Cleon and Demosthenes and told them that they were wasting their labor. But if they would give him some archers and light troops to go round to the enemy’s rear by a way he would undertake to find, he thought he could force the approach. When he had received what he asked for, he started from a point out of sight, so as not to be seen by the enemy. He crept on wherever the precipices of the island permitted, and where the Lacedaemonians, trusting to the strength of the ground, kept no guard. After the greatest difficulty he succeeded in getting round without being seen, and suddenly appeared on the high ground in their rear. The surprised enemy were dismayed, and his waiting friends were still more overjoyed. The Lacedaemonians were thus placed between two fires, and in the same dilemma (to compare small things with great) as at Thermopylae, where the defenders were cut off when the Persians got round by the path. Attacked now in front and behind, they began to give way, and, overcome by the odds against them and exhausted from want of food, they retreated.

The Athenians were already masters of the approaches. Cleon and Demosthenes saw that if the enemy gave way a single step further, their own soldiers would destroy them, and they put a stop to the battle and held their men back. They wished to take the Lacedaemonians alive to Athens, and hoped that their stubbornness might relax on hearing an offer of terms, and that they might surrender and yield to the present overwhelming danger. Proclamation was accordingly made, asking whether they would surrender themselves and their arms to the Athenians, to be dealt with at their discretion.

When the Lacedaemonians heard this offer, most of them lowered their shields and waved their hands to show that they accepted it. Hostilities now ceased, and a parley was held between Cleon and Demosthenes and, on the other side, Styphon, son of Pharax. Epitadas, the first of the previous commanders, had been killed, and Hippagretas, the next in command, had been left for dead among the slain, though still alive, so that the command had devolved upon Styphon according to the law, in case anything happened to his superiors. Styphon and his companions said they wished to send a herald to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland, to ask what they should do. The Athenians would not let any of them go, but themselves called for heralds from the mainland. After questions had been carried backwards and forwards two or three times, the last man who crossed over from the Lacedaemonians on the continent brought this message: “The Lacedaemonians bid you decide for yourselves, so long as you do nothing dishonorable.” After consulting together, they surrendered themselves and their arms. The Athenians guarded them that day and night. The next morning they set up a trophy on the island and got ready to sail, giving their prisoners in batches to be guarded by the captains of the galleys. The Lacedaemonians sent a herald and took up their dead. The number of the killed and of the prisoners taken on the island was as follows. Four hundred and twenty heavy infantry had crossed over; three hundred all but eight were taken alive to Athens, and the rest were killed. About a hundred and twenty of the prisoners were Spartans. The Athenian loss was small, since the battle had not been fought at close quarters.

The blockade in all, counting from the fight at sea to the battle on the island, had lasted seventy-two days. For twenty of these, while the envoys sent to treat for peace were away, the men had been given provisions; for the rest they were fed by the smugglers. Corn and other food were found on the island, for the commander Epitadas had kept the men on half rations. The Athenians and Peloponnesians now each withdrew their forces from Pylos and went home. Crazy as Cleon’s promise was, he fulfilled it, bringing the men to Athens within the twenty days, as he had pledged himself to do.

Nothing that happened in the war surprised the Hellenes so much as this. It was the opinion that no force or famine could make the Lacedaemonians give up their arms; they would fight on as best they could, and die with them in their hands. Indeed, people could scarcely believe that those who had surrendered were of the same stuff as the fallen. An Athenian ally, some time afterwards, insultingly asked one of the prisoners from the island whether those who had fallen were men of honor. He received the answer that the atraktos — that is, the arrow — would be worth a great deal if it could tell men of honor from the rest. This alluded to the fact that the killed were those whom the stones and the arrows happened to hit.

When the men arrived, the Athenians determined to keep them in prison until the peace, and, if the Peloponnesians invaded their country in the interval, to bring them out and put them to death. Meanwhile the defense of Pylos was not forgotten. The Messenians from Naupactus sent some of their likeliest men to their old country, to which Pylos formerly belonged, and began a series of incursions into Laconia, which their common dialect made most destructive. The Lacedaemonians had hitherto had no experience of incursions or of warfare of this kind. They found the Helots deserting and feared the spread of revolution in their country, and they began to be seriously uneasy. In spite of their unwillingness to betray this to the Athenians, they began to send envoys to Athens and tried to recover Pylos and the prisoners. The Athenians, however, kept grasping at more, and dismissed envoy after envoy without their having achieved anything. Such was the history of the affair of Pylos.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 13 — Seventh and Eighth Years of the War—End of Corcyraean Revolution— Peace of Gela—Capture of Nisaea
paragraphs: The same summer, directly after these events, the Athenians launched an expedition against Corinthian territory. They had eighty ships, two thousand Athenian heavy infantry, and two hundred cavalry carried on horse transports, with the Milesians, Andrians and Carystians of the allies in support. Nicias, son of Niceratus, commanded, with two colleagues. They put out to sea and at daybreak landed between Chersonese and Rheitus, on the beach below the Solygian hill. In old times the Dorians had settled on that hill and made war from it on the Aeolian inhabitants of Corinth, and a village called Solygia stands there now. The beach where the fleet came in is about a mile and a half from the village, seven miles from Corinth, and two and a quarter from the Isthmus. The Corinthians had heard from Argos that the Athenian armament was coming, and long before had gathered at the Isthmus, all except those who lived beyond it and five hundred who were away as garrison in Ambracia and Leucadia. They were there in full force, watching for the Athenians to land. But the Athenians slipped past them by arriving in the dark. The Corinthians were told by signals, left half their number at Cenchreae in case the Athenians should go against Crommyon, and marched in all haste to meet the landing.

Battus, one of the two generals present at the action, took a company to defend the village of Solygia, which had no fortifications, while Lycophron stayed to give battle with the rest. The Corinthians first attacked the Athenian right wing, which had just landed in front of Chersonese, and then the rest of the army. The battle was stubborn and was fought hand to hand throughout. The Athenians and Carystians of the right wing, who had been placed at the end of the line, withstood the Corinthians and with some difficulty drove them back. The Corinthians retreated to a wall on the rising ground behind, threw stones down on their enemies, and then came on again singing the paean. The Athenians received them, and they were again engaged at close quarters. At this moment a Corinthian company came to the relief of the left wing, routed the Athenian right and chased it down to the sea. From the ships, however, the Athenians and Carystians drove the Corinthians back in their turn. Meanwhile the rest of the army on either side fought on tenaciously, above all the Corinthian right wing, where Lycophron held out against the Athenian left. It was feared that this left might make an attempt on the village of Solygia.

For a long time neither side gave way. Then the Athenians, helped by their cavalry (the enemy had none), at length routed the Corinthians, who withdrew to the hill and halted there, and did not come down again. It was in this rout of their right wing that they lost the most men, and Lycophron their general was among the dead. The rest of the army was broken and put to flight in the same way, but without being seriously pursued or pressed, and it retired to the high ground and took up its position there. The Athenians saw that the enemy no longer offered battle. They stripped his dead, took up their own, and immediately set up a trophy. Meanwhile the half of the Corinthians who had been left at Cenchreae to guard against an Athenian landing at Crommyon could not see the battle because of Mount Oneion, but learned what was happening from the dust and hurried to the rescue. So did the older Corinthians from the town, when they discovered what had occurred. The Athenians saw them all coming against them and thought they were reinforcements arriving from the neighboring Peloponnesians. They withdrew in haste to their ships with their spoils and their own dead, except two whom they could not find and so left behind. They went on board and crossed over to the islands opposite, and from there sent a herald and recovered under truce the bodies they had left. Two hundred and twelve Corinthians fell in the battle, and rather fewer than fifty Athenians.

The Athenians weighed anchor from the islands and sailed the same day to Crommyon in Corinthian territory, about thirteen miles from the city. They anchored there, laid waste the country, and spent the night. The next day they first coasted along to the territory of Epidaurus and made a landing there. Then they came to Methana, between Epidaurus and Troezen, and drew a wall across the isthmus of the peninsula and fortified it. They left a post there, from which raids were afterwards made on the country of Troezen, Haliae and Epidaurus. When they had walled off this spot, the fleet sailed home.

While these events were going on, Eurymedon and Sophocles had put to sea with the Athenian fleet from Pylos on their way to Sicily. They arrived at Corcyra and joined the townsmen in an expedition against the party established on Mount Istone. As I have mentioned, this party had crossed over after the revolution and become masters of the country, to the great harm of the inhabitants. Their stronghold was taken by assault, and the garrison took refuge in a body on some high ground and capitulated there. They agreed to give up their mercenary auxiliaries, to lay down their arms, and to submit themselves to the discretion of the Athenian people. The generals carried them across under truce to the island of Ptychia, to be held in custody until they could be sent to Athens. It was agreed that if any of them were caught trying to escape, all would lose the benefit of the treaty. Meanwhile the leaders of the Corcyraean commons were afraid that the Athenians might spare the lives of the prisoners, and they resorted to the following stratagem. They won over a few of the men on the island by secretly sending friends to them, with instructions to provide them with a boat and to tell them, as if for their own sakes, that they had best escape as quickly as possible, since the Athenian generals were going to hand them over to the Corcyraean people.

These representations succeeded. It was arranged that the men were caught sailing out in the boat that had been provided, and so the treaty became void and the whole body was handed over to the Corcyraeans. The Athenian generals were in great part responsible for this result. They plainly did not want to sail for Sicily, and so leave to others the honor of conducting the men to Athens. This encouraged the intriguers in their design and seemed to confirm what they had told the prisoners. The Corcyraeans shut up the prisoners thus handed over in a large building. Afterwards they took them out by twenties, bound together, and led them past two lines of heavy infantry, one on each side. The men in the lines beat and stabbed any prisoner they saw to be a personal enemy, while men carrying whips walked beside the column and hurried along those who went too slowly.

As many as sixty men were taken out and killed in this way without the knowledge of their friends in the building, who fancied they were merely being moved from one prison to another. At last, however, someone opened their eyes to the truth. They then called on the Athenians to kill them themselves, if that was their pleasure, refused to go out of the building any longer, and said they would do all they could to prevent anyone coming in. The Corcyraeans did not wish to force a passage through the doors themselves. They climbed on top of the building, broke through the roof, threw down the tiles, and shot arrows at the prisoners, who sheltered from them as well as they could. Most of the prisoners, meanwhile, were busy killing themselves, driving into their throats the arrows shot by the enemy, and hanging themselves with cords taken from some beds that happened to be there and with strips torn from their clothing. In short, they adopted every possible means of self-destruction, and they also fell victim to the missiles of their enemies on the roof. Night came on while these horrors were being enacted, and most of it had passed before they were over. When it was day, the Corcyraeans threw the bodies in layers onto wagons and carried them out of the city. All the women taken in the stronghold were sold as slaves. In this way the Corcyraeans of the mountain were destroyed by the commons. And so, after terrible excesses, the party strife came to an end, at least as far as the period of this war is concerned, for of one party there was practically nothing left. Meanwhile the Athenians sailed off to Sicily, their original destination, and carried on the war there with their allies.

At the close of the summer, the Athenians at Naupactus and the Acarnanians made an expedition against Anactorium, the Corinthian town at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, and took it by treachery. The Acarnanians themselves then sent settlers from all parts of Acarnania and occupied the place.

Summer was now over. During the winter that followed, Aristides, son of Archippus, who was one of the commanders of the Athenian ships sent to collect money from the allies, arrested a Persian named Artaphernes at Eion, on the Strymon. Artaphernes was on his way from the King to Lacedaemon. He was taken to Athens, where the Athenians had his dispatches translated from the Assyrian script and read them. The letter touched on many other subjects, but in substance it told the Lacedaemonians that the King did not know what they wanted, since of the many ambassadors they had sent him no two ever told the same story. If, however, they were prepared to speak plainly, they might send him some envoys with this Persian. Afterwards the Athenians sent Artaphernes back to Ephesus in a galley, and ambassadors with him. There they heard of the death of King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, which had taken place about that time, and so they returned home.

The same winter the Chians pulled down their new wall at the command of the Athenians, who suspected them of planning an insurrection. They first obtained pledges from the Athenians, and such security as was possible, that they would go on being treated as before. Thus the winter ended, and with it ended the seventh year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

In the first days of the next summer there was an eclipse of the sun at the time of the new moon, and early in the same month an earthquake. Meanwhile the Mitylenian and other Lesbian exiles set out, mostly from the continent, with mercenaries hired in Peloponnese and others raised on the spot. They took Rhoeteum, but restored it undamaged on receiving two thousand Phocaean staters. After this they marched against Antandrus and took the town by treachery. Their plan was to free Antandrus and the rest of the Actaean towns, which had formerly belonged to Mitylene but were now held by the Athenians. Once fortified there, they would have every facility for building ships, since Ida was near and timber therefore plentiful, and plenty of other supplies besides. From this base they could easily ravage Lesbos, which was not far off, and make themselves masters of the Aeolian towns on the continent.

While the exiles were making these plans, the Athenians in the same summer made an expedition against Cythera with sixty ships, two thousand heavy infantry, a few cavalry, and some allied troops from Miletus and other places. The commanders were Nicias, son of Niceratus, Nicostratus, son of Diotrephes, and Autocles, son of Tolmaeus. Cythera is an island lying off Laconia, opposite Malea. Its inhabitants are Lacedaemonians of the class of the Perioeci, and an officer called the judge of Cythera went over to the place every year from Sparta. A garrison of heavy infantry was also regularly sent there, and great attention was paid to the island. It was the landing place for merchant ships from Egypt and Libya, and it also protected Laconia from raids by pirates from the sea at the only point where Laconia can be attacked, since the whole coast rises abruptly toward the Sicilian and Cretan seas.

The Athenians came to land with their armament. With ten ships and two thousand Milesian heavy infantry they took the town of Scandea, on the sea. With the rest of their forces they landed on the side of the island facing Malea and went against the lower town of Cythera, where they found all the inhabitants encamped. A battle followed. The Cytherians held their ground for a short while, then turned and fled into the upper town, and soon afterwards capitulated to Nicias and his colleagues. They agreed to leave their fate to the decision of the Athenians, with only their lives guaranteed. Nicias had previously been in correspondence with some of the inhabitants, and this made the surrender quicker and gave the Cytherians better terms, both then and later. Otherwise the Athenians would have expelled them, because they were Lacedaemonians and their island lay so near Laconia. After the capitulation the Athenians occupied the town of Scandea, near the harbor, and appointed a garrison for Cythera. They then sailed to Asine, Helus and most of the places on the sea, made landings, camped for the night on shore at convenient spots, and went on ravaging the country for about seven days.

The Lacedaemonians saw the Athenians masters of Cythera and expected landings of the same kind on their coasts. They nowhere opposed them in force, but sent garrisons here and there through the country, each made up of as many heavy infantry as the threatened points seemed to require, and for the most part kept strictly on the defensive. They had suffered a severe and unexpected blow on the island, Pylos and Cythera were occupied, and on every side they saw a war whose rapidity defied precaution. They lived in constant fear of internal revolution, and now took the unusual step of raising four hundred horse and a force of archers. They became more timid than ever in military matters, since they found themselves involved in a naval struggle, which their organization had never contemplated, and against Athenians, who always counted an enterprise left unattempted as a success thrown away. Besides this, their numerous recent reverses, coming one upon another without any reason, had thoroughly unnerved them. They were always afraid of a second disaster like that on the island, and so scarcely dared to take the field. They fancied that they could not make a move without a blunder, for they were new to the experience of adversity and had lost all confidence in themselves.

Accordingly they now let the Athenians ravage their seaboard without making any move. The garrison in whose neighborhood a landing was made always thought its numbers insufficient and shared the general feeling. A single garrison, near Cotyrta and Aphrodisia, did venture to resist. Its charge struck terror into the scattered mob of light troops, but when it was met by the heavy infantry it retreated, with the loss of a few men and some arms. The Athenians set up a trophy for this and then sailed off to Cythera. From there they sailed round to Epidaurus Limera, ravaged part of the country, and so came to Thyrea in the Cynurian territory, on the border between Argos and Laconia. The Lacedaemonians who owned this district had given it to the expelled Aeginetans to live in. They did so in return for the Aeginetans’ good services at the time of the earthquake and the rising of the Helots, and also because, although subjects of Athens, the Aeginetans had always sided with Lacedaemon.

While the Athenians were still at sea, the Aeginetans abandoned a fort they were building on the coast and retreated into the upper town where they lived, rather more than a mile from the sea. One of the Lacedaemonian district garrisons, which was helping them with the work, refused to enter the town with them, though they begged it to. It thought it dangerous to shut itself up within the wall, and it withdrew to the high ground and kept quiet, not considering itself a match for the enemy. Meanwhile the Athenians landed, advanced at once with all their forces, and took Thyrea. They burned the town and plundered what was in it. The Aeginetans who were not killed in the fighting they took with them to Athens, together with Tantalus, son of Patrocles, their Lacedaemonian commander, who had been wounded and taken prisoner. They also took with them a few men from Cythera whom they thought it safest to remove. The Athenians decided to lodge these in the islands. The rest of the Cytherians were to keep their lands and pay four talents tribute. The captured Aeginetans were all to be put to death, because of the old inveterate feud, and Tantalus was to share the imprisonment of the Lacedaemonians taken on the island.

The same summer, the inhabitants of Camarina and Gela in Sicily first made an armistice with each other. After this, embassies from all the other Sicilian cities assembled at Gela to try to bring about a pacification. Many opinions were expressed on one side and the other, according to the grievances and claims of the different parties. Then Hermocrates, son of Hermon, a Syracusan and the most influential man among them, addressed the assembly in these words:

“Sicilians, if I speak now, it is not because my city is the least in Sicily or the one that has suffered most from the war. I speak in order to state publicly what seems to me the best policy for the whole island. That war is an evil is so familiar to everyone that it would be tedious to argue it at length. No one is forced into war by ignorance, or kept out of it by fear, if he fancies there is something to be gained by it. To the first, the gain looks greater than the danger. The second would rather run the risk than put up with any immediate sacrifice. But if both should happen to have chosen the wrong moment for acting in this way, advice to make peace would not be unhelpful. And this, if we would only see it, is exactly what we most need at the present juncture.

“I suppose that no one will dispute that we went to war at first to serve our own separate interests, that we are now debating, in view of the same interests, how we can make peace, and that if we part without having what we think our rights, we shall go to war again. And yet, as men of sense, we ought to see that our separate interests are not the only thing at stake in this congress. There is also the question whether we still have time to save Sicily, the whole of which, in my opinion, is menaced by Athenian ambition. We ought to find in the very name of that people more compelling arguments for peace than any I can offer. We see the first power in Hellas watching our mistakes with the few ships she has at present in our waters. Under the fair name of alliance, she speciously seeks to turn to account the natural hostility that exists between us. Suppose we go to war and call in to help us a people who are ready enough to carry their arms even where they are not invited. Suppose we injure ourselves at our own expense and at the same time serve as the pioneers of their dominion. Then we may expect that when they see us worn out they will one day come with a larger armament and try to bring all of us into subjection.

“And yet, if we as sensible men call in allies and court danger, it should be to enrich our different countries with new acquisitions, and not to ruin what they already possess. We should understand that internal discord, which is so fatal to communities in general, will be equally fatal to Sicily if we, its inhabitants, absorbed in our local quarrels, neglect the common enemy. These considerations should reconcile individual with individual and city with city, and unite us in a common effort to save the whole of Sicily. Nor should anyone imagine that only the Dorians are enemies of Athens, while the Chalcidian race is secured by its Ionian blood. The attack in question is not inspired by hatred of one of two nationalities, but by a desire for the good things of Sicily, which belong to all of us in common. This is proved by the way Athens received the Chalcidian invitation. An ally who has never given them any assistance whatever at once receives from them almost more than the treaty entitles him to. That the Athenians should cherish this ambition and follow this policy is very excusable. I do not blame those who wish to rule, but those who are over-ready to serve. It is just as much in men’s nature to rule those who submit to them as it is to resist those who molest them. The one is no less invariable than the other. Meanwhile all who see these dangers and refuse to provide against them properly are mistaken, and so are those who have come here without having made up their minds that our first duty is to unite to be rid of the common peril. The quickest way to be rid of it is to make peace with each other, since the Athenians menace us not from their own country but from the country of those who invited them here. In this way, instead of war issuing in war, peace quietly ends our quarrels. And the guests who come here under fair pretenses for bad ends will have good reason to go away without having attained them.

“So far as the Athenians are concerned, such are the great advantages shown to lie in a wise policy. Apart from this, there is the universal agreement that peace is the first of blessings. How then can we refuse to make it among ourselves? Or do you not think that the good you have, and the ills you complain of, would be better preserved and cured by quiet than by war? Peace has its honors and splendors, less perilous than those of war, not to mention the many other blessings one might dwell on, as one might dwell on the equally many miseries of war. These considerations should teach you not to disregard my words, but rather to look in them, each of you, for his own safety. Suppose there is anyone here who feels certain, whether by right or by might, of achieving his object. Let him not find this surprise too severe a disappointment. Let him remember that many before now have tried to chastise a wrongdoer and, failing to punish their enemy, have not even saved themselves. And many who have trusted in force to gain an advantage have, instead of gaining anything more, been doomed to lose what they had. Vengeance is not necessarily successful because wrong has been done, nor is strength sure because it is confident. The incalculable element in the future exercises the widest influence. It is the most treacherous of all things, and yet in fact the most useful, since it frightens us all equally and so makes us think before we attack each other.

“Let us therefore now allow the undefined fear of this unknown future, and the immediate terror of the Athenians’ presence, to have their natural effect. Let us regard any failure to carry out the programs that we may each have sketched out for ourselves as sufficiently accounted for by these obstacles, and let us send the intruder away from the country. If everlasting peace is impossible between us, let us at all events make a treaty for as long a term as possible, and put off our private differences to another day. In short, let us recognize that if we adopt my advice we shall each remain citizens of a free state, and as such arbiters of our own destiny, able to return good or bad offices with equal effect. If we reject it, we shall depend on others. We shall then be not only powerless to repel an insult, but, on the most favorable supposition, friends to our direst enemies and at feud with our natural friends.

“For myself, though, as I said at first, I represent a great city and am able to think less of defending myself than of attacking others, I am prepared to concede something in anticipation of these dangers. I am not inclined to ruin myself for the sake of hurting my enemies, nor so blinded by animosity as to think myself as much master of fortune, which I cannot command, as I am of my own plans. But I am ready to give up anything reasonable. I call upon the rest of you to follow my example of your own free will, without being forced to it by the enemy. There is no disgrace in kinsmen giving way to one another, a Dorian to a Dorian, or a Chalcidian to his brethren. Beyond this, we are neighbors, we live in the same country, we are girt by the same sea, and we go by the same name of Sicilians. We shall go to war again, I suppose, when the time comes, and again make peace among ourselves by means of future congresses. But the foreign invader, if we are wise, will always find us united against him, since the hurt of one is the danger of all. And we shall never in future invite into the island either allies or mediators. By so acting we shall at the present moment do Sicily a double service, ridding her at once of the Athenians and of civil war, and in future we shall live in freedom at home and be less menaced from abroad.”

Such were the words of Hermocrates. The Sicilians took his advice and came to an understanding among themselves to end the war, each keeping what they had. The Camarinaeans were to take Morgantina at a price fixed to be paid to the Syracusans. The allies of the Athenians then called the commanding officers and told them that they were going to make peace and that they would be included in the treaty. The generals assented, the peace was concluded, and the Athenian fleet afterwards sailed away from Sicily. When the generals arrived at Athens, the Athenians banished Pythodorus and Sophocles, and fined Eurymedon, for having taken bribes to depart when they might have subdued Sicily. So thoroughly had their present prosperity persuaded the citizens that nothing could withstand them, and that they could achieve what was possible and impracticable alike, whether their means were ample or inadequate. The secret of this was their general extraordinary success, which made them confuse their strength with their hopes.

The same summer the Megarians in the city were pressed by the hostilities of the Athenians, who invaded their country twice every year with all their forces. They were also harassed by the raids of their own exiles at Pegae, who had been expelled in a revolution by the popular party. They began to ask each other whether it would not be better to receive back their exiles and so free the town from one of its two scourges. The friends of the exiles saw the agitation and now demanded this proposal more openly than before. The leaders of the commons saw that the sufferings of the times had worn out the constancy of their supporters. In their alarm they entered into correspondence with the Athenian generals, Hippocrates, son of Ariphron, and Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and resolved to betray the town, thinking this less dangerous to themselves than the return of the party they had banished. It was accordingly arranged that the Athenians should first take the long walls, which extend for nearly a mile from the city to the port of Nisaea. This was to prevent the Peloponnesians coming to the rescue from Nisaea, where they were the sole garrison securing the fidelity of Megara. After this, an attempt was to be made to put the upper town into their hands, which it was thought would then come over with less difficulty.

Plans had been settled between the Athenians and their correspondents, both for what was to be said and for what was to be done. The Athenians then sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under Hippocrates, and took post in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be dug for the walls. Demosthenes, the other commander, placed himself in ambush with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it that night except those whose business it was to know. A little before daybreak the traitors in Megara began to act. For a long time they had been in the habit, every night, of carrying a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and sailing out in it, under pretense of marauding. This gave them a means of opening the gates, and they did it with the consent of the officer in command. They brought the boat back on the cart before day and took it inside the wall through the gates. Their pretended aim was to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbor. On this occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat. The Athenians, who had agreed on this with the traitors, saw it and ran from the ambush at top speed, to reach the gates before they were shut again and while the cart was still there to keep them from closing. At the same moment their Megarian accomplices killed the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, at the very spot where the trophy now stands. He was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and so secured the gates for the Athenian heavy infantry coming up.

After this, each of the Athenians, as fast as he entered, went against the wall. A few of the Peloponnesian garrison at first stood their ground and tried to repel the assault, and some of them were killed. But the main body took fright and fled. The night attack, and the sight of the Megarian traitors in arms against them, made them think that all Megara had gone over to the enemy. It also happened that the Athenian herald, on his own idea, called out and invited any Megarians who wished to join the Athenian ranks. The garrison no sooner heard this than they gave way. Convinced that they were the victims of a concerted attack, they took refuge in Nisaea. By daybreak the walls were taken and the Megarians in the city were in great agitation. The persons who had negotiated with the Athenians, supported by the rest of the popular party, which was privy to the plot, then said that the gates ought to be opened and the people should march out to battle. It had been agreed between them that the Athenians should rush in the moment the gates were opened, while the conspirators would be distinguished from the rest by being anointed with oil, so as to avoid being hurt. They could open the gates with more security because four thousand Athenian heavy infantry from Eleusis and six hundred horse had marched all night, according to the agreement, and were now close at hand. The conspirators were all anointed and at their posts by the gates, when one of their accomplices denounced the plot to the opposite party. These gathered together and came in a body. They said bluntly that the people must not march out, a thing they had never yet ventured even when in greater force than at present, nor wantonly compromise the safety of the town, and that if their advice was not heeded, the battle would have to be fought in Megara itself. For the rest, they gave no sign that they knew of the intrigue, but stoutly maintained that their advice was the best. Meanwhile they kept close by and watched the gates, which made it impossible for the conspirators to carry out their purpose.

The Athenian generals saw that some obstacle had arisen and that taking the town by force was no longer practicable. They at once proceeded to invest Nisaea, thinking that if they could take it before relief arrived, the surrender of Megara would soon follow. Iron, stone-masons and everything else required came up quickly from Athens. Starting from the wall they occupied, the Athenians built a cross wall facing Megara, down to the sea on either side of Nisaea. The ditch and the walls were divided among the army. Stones and bricks were taken from the suburb, and the fruit-trees and timber were cut down to make a palisade wherever one seemed necessary. The houses in the suburb, with battlements added, sometimes also became part of the fortification. The work continued the whole of that day, and by the afternoon of the next the wall was all but complete. Then the garrison in Nisaea capitulated to the Athenians. They were alarmed by their complete lack of provisions, which they had been used to take in for the day from the upper town. They did not expect any speedy relief from the Peloponnesians, and they supposed Megara to be hostile. The condition was that they should give up their arms and each be ransomed for a stipulated sum, while their Lacedaemonian commander, and any others of his countrymen in the place, were left to the discretion of the Athenians. On these conditions they surrendered and came out. The Athenians broke down the long walls at their point of junction with Megara, took possession of Nisaea, and went on with their other preparations.

Just at this time the Lacedaemonian Brasidas, son of Tellis, happened to be in the neighborhood of Sicyon and Corinth, getting ready an army for Thrace. As soon as he heard that the walls had been taken, he feared for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and for the safety of Megara. He sent to the Boeotians to meet him as quickly as possible at Tripodiscus, a village of the Megarid so called, under Mount Geraneia. He went there himself with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian heavy infantry, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and such troops of his own as he had already levied, expecting to find Nisaea not yet taken. Hearing of its fall (he had marched out by night to Tripodiscus), he took three hundred picked men from the army without waiting until his coming should be known, and came up to Megara unobserved by the Athenians, who were down by the sea. His purpose was, ostensibly, and really if possible, to make an attempt on Nisaea, but above all to get into Megara and secure the town. He accordingly invited the townspeople to admit his party, saying that he had hopes of recovering Nisaea.

However, one of the Megarian factions feared that he might expel them and restore the exiles. The other feared that the commons, apprehensive of this very danger, might set upon them, and that the city would then be destroyed by a battle within its gates, under the eyes of the Athenians lying in ambush. He was accordingly refused admittance. Both parties chose to remain quiet and await the event, each expecting a battle between the Athenians and the relieving army, and each thinking it safer to see its friends victorious before declaring in their favor.

Unable to carry his point, Brasidas went back to the rest of the army. At daybreak the Boeotians joined him. They had determined to relieve Megara, whose danger they considered their own, even before hearing from Brasidas, and were already in full force at Plataea when his messenger arrived to add spurs to their resolution. They at once sent on to him two thousand two hundred heavy infantry and six hundred horse, and returned home with the main body. The whole army thus assembled numbered six thousand heavy infantry. The Athenian heavy infantry were drawn up by Nisaea and the sea. But their light troops were scattered over the plain, and the Boeotian horse attacked them and drove them to the sea. They were taken entirely by surprise, since on previous occasions no relief had ever come to the Megarians from any quarter. Here the Boeotians were in their turn charged and engaged by the Athenian horse, and a cavalry action followed which lasted a long time, and in which both parties claimed the victory. The Athenians killed and stripped the leader of the Boeotian horse, together with a few of his comrades who had charged right up to Nisaea. They remained masters of the bodies, gave them back under truce, and set up a trophy. But in the action as a whole the forces separated without either side having gained a decisive advantage, the Boeotians returning to their army and the Athenians to Nisaea.

After this Brasidas and the army came nearer to the sea and to Megara. They took up a convenient position and remained quiet in order of battle, expecting to be attacked by the Athenians and knowing that the Megarians were waiting to see which side would be the victor. This attitude seemed to offer two advantages. They did not take the offensive or willingly provoke the hazards of a battle, yet they openly showed their readiness to fight, and so would fairly reap the honors of the day without bearing its burden. At the same time they effectively served their interests at Megara. For if they had failed to show themselves, they would not have had a chance, but would certainly have been considered vanquished and would have lost the town. As it was, the Athenians might possibly not be inclined to accept their challenge, and their object would be attained without fighting. And so it turned out. The Athenians formed outside the long walls and, since the enemy did not attack, stood there motionless. Their generals had decided that the risk was too unequal. In fact most of their objects had already been attained. They would have to begin a battle against superior numbers, and if victorious could only gain Megara, while a defeat would destroy the flower of their heavy soldiery. For the enemy it was different. Even the states actually represented in his army each risked only a part of its entire force, so he might well be more audacious. Accordingly, after waiting for some time without either side attacking, the Athenians withdrew to Nisaea, and the Peloponnesians after them to the point from which they had set out. The friends of the Megarian exiles now threw aside their hesitation. They looked upon Brasidas as the victor and upon the Athenians as having declined the battle, and so they opened the gates to him and to the commanders from the different states, received them into the town and proceeded to discuss matters with them. The party in correspondence with the Athenians was paralyzed by the turn things had taken.

Afterwards Brasidas let the allies go home and went back himself to Corinth, to prepare for his expedition to Thrace, his original destination. The Athenians also returned home. The Megarians in the city who were most implicated in the Athenian negotiation knew that they had been detected, and presently disappeared. The rest conferred with the friends of the exiles and restored the party at Pegae, after binding them under solemn oaths to take no vengeance for the past and only to consult the real interests of the town. However, as soon as these men were in office, they held a review of the heavy infantry. They separated the battalions and picked out about a hundred of their enemies, those thought to be most involved in the correspondence with the Athenians. They brought them before the people and compelled the vote to be given openly, and had them condemned and executed, and established a close oligarchy in the town. This revolution lasted a very long while, although effected by a very few partisans.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 14 — Eighth and Ninth Years of the War—Invasion of Boeotia—Fall of Amphipolis—Brilliant Successes of Brasidas
paragraphs: The same summer the Mitylenians were about to fortify Antandrus, as they had intended. But Demodocus and Aristides, who commanded the Athenian squadron collecting subsidies, heard on the Hellespont what was being done there (their colleague Lamachus had sailed into the Pontus with ten ships). They feared that the place would become a second Anaia — the town where the Samian exiles had settled to harass Samos, where they helped the Peloponnesians by sending pilots to their navy, and where they kept the city in agitation by receiving all its outlaws. So they gathered a force from the allies and sailed against Antandrus, defeated the troops that came out to meet them, and recovered the place. Not long afterwards Lamachus, who had sailed into the Pontus, lost his ships at anchor in the river Calex, in the territory of Heraclea. Rain had fallen in the interior, and the flood came down suddenly upon them. He and his men then went by land through the Bithynian Thracians on the Asiatic side and reached Chalcedon, the Megarian colony at the mouth of the Pontus.

The same summer the Athenian general Demosthenes arrived at Naupactus with forty ships, immediately after the return from the Megarid. Certain men in the cities of Boeotia, who wished to change their constitution and introduce a democracy like the one at Athens, had made overtures to Hippocrates and to him. Ptoeodorus, a Theban exile, was the chief mover in this intrigue. One party was to betray to them Siphae, the seaport in the bay of Crisae, in Thespian territory. Another party was to put Chaeronea into their hands. (Chaeronea is a dependency of the city once called the Minyan, now the Boeotian, Orchomenus.) The exiles from that town were very active in the business and were hiring men in Peloponnese. Some Phocians were also in the plot, since Chaeronea is the frontier town of Boeotia and lies close to Phanotis in Phocia. Meanwhile the Athenians were to seize Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo in the territory of Tanagra, facing Euboea. All these things were to happen at once, on an appointed day, so that the Boeotians could not unite to oppose them at Delium, being kept busy everywhere by disturbances at home. If the enterprise succeeded and Delium was fortified, its authors confidently expected that things would not stay as they were, even if no revolution followed at once in Boeotia. With these places in their hands, the country harassed by raids, and a refuge always near for the partisans who took part in them, the rebels would be supported by the Athenians and the forces of the oligarchs would be divided. After a while it would then be possible to settle matters as they wished.

Such was the plot in contemplation. Hippocrates, with a force raised at home, waited for the right moment to take the field against the Boeotians. He sent Demosthenes ahead with the forty ships to Naupactus, to raise an army of Acarnanians and other allies in that region and then sail to receive Siphae from the conspirators. A day had been agreed for both operations to take place together. When Demosthenes arrived, he found that the united Acarnanians had already forced Oeniadae to join the Athenian confederacy. He raised all the allies in those countries himself, marched against Salynthius and the Agraeans, and subdued them. After that he turned to the preparations he needed to be at Siphae by the appointed time.

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march to the Thracian places with seventeen hundred heavy infantry. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, he sent a messenger from there to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to conduct him and his army through the country. So there came to Melitia in Achaia Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, and under their escort he resumed his march. Other Thessalians accompanied him as well, among them Niconidas from Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to cross Thessaly without an escort, and throughout Hellas it was a delicate step for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbor’s country. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians. Indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to go on, since even as it was he was met at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. His escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will; they were only friends attending an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, that his arms were directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war, and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and the Lacedaemonians to prevent the two nations from having access to each other’s territory, he neither would nor could go on against their wishes; he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away. He then took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. So on the very day he set out from Melitia he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus. From there he went on to Phacium, and from Phacium to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas. Dium is a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, facing Thessaly.

In this way Brasidas hurried through Thessaly before anyone could get ready to stop him, and reached Perdiccas and Chalcidice. The army had been brought out of Peloponnese by the Thracian towns in revolt against Athens and by Perdiccas, who was alarmed at the Athenian successes. The Chalcidians thought they would be the first target of an Athenian expedition. (Not that the neighboring towns which had not yet revolted were not also secretly party to the invitation.) Perdiccas, for his part, had fears of his own because of his old quarrels with the Athenians, although he was not openly at war with them, and above all he wished to reduce Arrhabaeus, king of the Lyncestians. It had been less difficult for them to get an army to leave Peloponnese because of the Lacedaemonians’ ill fortune at the present moment. The Athenian attacks upon Peloponnese, and in particular upon Laconia, might, it was hoped, be diverted most effectively by annoying the Athenians in return, and by sending an army to their allies, especially as these were willing to maintain it and had asked for it to aid them in revolting. The Lacedaemonians were also glad to have an excuse for sending some of the Helots out of the country, for fear that the present state of affairs and the occupation of Pylos might encourage them to rise. Indeed, fear of the Helots’ numbers and obstinacy even persuaded the Lacedaemonians to the action which I shall now relate; their policy had always been governed by the need to take precautions against them. The Helots were invited by proclamation to pick out those of their number who claimed to have distinguished themselves most against the enemy, so that they might receive their freedom. The aim was to test them, since it was thought that the first to claim their freedom would be the most high-spirited and the most likely to rebel. As many as two thousand were selected in this way. They crowned themselves and went round the temples, rejoicing in their new freedom. The Spartans, however, did away with them soon afterwards, and no one ever knew how each of them perished. So the Spartans now gladly sent seven hundred Helots as heavy infantry with Brasidas, who recruited the rest of his force with money in Peloponnese.

Brasidas himself was sent out by the Lacedaemonians mainly at his own desire, although the Chalcidians were also eager to have him. He had shown himself a thorough man whenever anything had to be done at Sparta, and his later service abroad proved of the utmost use to his country. At the present moment his just and moderate conduct toward the towns generally succeeded in procuring their revolt, besides the places he managed to take by treachery. So when the Lacedaemonians wished to treat, as they ultimately did, they had places to offer in exchange, and meanwhile the burden of war was lifted from Peloponnese. Later in the war, after the events in Sicily, it was the valor and conduct Brasidas showed at this time, known by experience to some and by hearsay to others, that chiefly created among the allies of Athens a feeling for the Lacedaemonians. He was the first to go out and show himself so good a man in every respect that he left behind the conviction that the rest were like him.

Meanwhile the Athenians learned of his arrival in the Thracian country, and no sooner had they heard of it than they declared war against Perdiccas, whom they regarded as the author of the expedition, and kept a closer watch on their allies in that quarter.

Upon the arrival of Brasidas and his army, Perdiccas immediately set out with them and with his own forces against his neighbor Arrhabaeus, son of Bromerus, king of the Lyncestian Macedonians. He had a quarrel with him and wished to subdue him. But when he reached the pass leading into Lyncus with his army and Brasidas, Brasidas told him that before starting hostilities he wished to go and try to persuade Arrhabaeus to become an ally of Lacedaemon. Arrhabaeus had already made overtures, saying he was willing to make Brasidas arbitrator between them. The Chalcidian envoys who accompanied Brasidas had also warned him not to remove the apprehensions of Perdiccas, so as to ensure his greater zeal in their cause. Besides, the envoys of Perdiccas had talked at Lacedaemon about his bringing many of the places around him into alliance with them; and so Brasidas thought he might take a larger view of the question of Arrhabaeus. Perdiccas retorted that he had not brought him along to arbitrate in their quarrel, but to put down the enemies he might point out to him, and that while he, Perdiccas, maintained half the army, it was a breach of faith for Brasidas to parley with Arrhabaeus. Nevertheless Brasidas disregarded the wishes of Perdiccas and held the parley in spite of him, and let himself be persuaded to lead the army away without invading the country of Arrhabaeus. After this Perdiccas, holding that faith had not been kept with him, contributed only a third instead of half of the support of the army.

That same summer Brasidas lost no time. A little before the vintage he marched with the Chalcidians against Acanthus, a colony of the Andrians. The people of the town were split over whether to receive him: on one side were those who had joined the Chalcidians in inviting him, on the other the popular party. Still, fear for their fruit, which was not yet gathered, let Brasidas persuade the multitude to let him in alone and hear him before deciding. He was admitted and came before the people, and, as a speaker not bad for a Lacedaemonian, he addressed them as follows:

“Acanthians, the Lacedaemonians have sent me and my army to make good the reason we gave when we began the war: that we were fighting the Athenians in order to free Hellas. If we have been slow to come, the cause was a mistaken hope about how the war at home would go. We expected to bring the Athenians down quickly by our own efforts alone, with no risk to you, and you must not blame us for that. We have come as soon as we could, and we mean, with your help, to do our best to subdue them. Meanwhile it astonishes me to find your gates closed against me and no better welcome waiting. We Lacedaemonians took you for allies who were eager for us, and thought we would be with you in spirit before we ever arrived in body. That is why we accepted every risk of a march of many days through a strange country: our zeal carried us that far. It would be a terrible thing if you now had other plans, and meant to block your own freedom and that of Hellas. You do more than oppose me yourselves. Wherever I go, people will be less ready to join me, because you, the first to whom I came — a considerable town like Acanthus, and men as prudent as the Acanthians — refused to receive me. I shall then have nothing to prove that the reason I give is the true one. People will say either that the freedom I offer is somehow unfair, or that my force is too weak to protect you if Athens attacks. Yet when I went with this same army to relieve Nisaea, the Athenians had the larger force and still did not dare to engage me. It is unlikely that they will ever send across the sea against you an army as large as the one they had at Nisaea. As for me, I have not come to hurt the Hellenes but to free them. The solemn oaths by which I have bound my government, that every ally I bring over shall be independent, bear witness to it. And I do not come to win your alliance by force or by fraud. I come to offer you mine, to help you against your Athenian masters. After the guarantees I offer, then, I protest against any suspicion of my intentions, and equally against any doubt of my power to protect you; and I invite you to join me without hesitation.
